title: Computational Advertising for Meaningful Brands, the Public Purpose, and a Sustainable Ecology: A Call for Research into a Systems Approach and Modeling Applications of LLMs in Marketing and Advertising
venue: Journal of Current Issues & Research in Advertising
authors: Stewart Pearson
keywords: large language models; advertising; marketing; brand building; online advertising; digital platforms; triple bottom line; system dynamics modeling; sustainable economy; public purpose; environmental impact of advertising; business innovation; AI in advertising; Marketing and Advertising Strategies; Digital Marketing and Social Media; Advertising and Communication Studies
abstract: Technology and computation in 2024 are dominated by applications of artificial intelligence (AI) and large language models (LLMs). The domains of marketing and advertising have already been transformed over the past 30 years by the internet, data, and digital technologies. Practitioners and scholars are focused on AI and LLMs as the drivers of the next paradigm shift in communication and advertising. Both constituencies are aligned on the primary goal of advertising to create economic growth by building brands with differentiation and meaning that contribute to corporate financial valuations. This paper notes the failure of digital advertising to build brands over the past three decades, while economic value in markets has been usurped by digital platforms. Further, scholars question the wider impact of digital advertising on society and the environment. This paper presents a positive vision for marketing and advertising enabled by LLMs. It envisions advertising’s goals redefined for a “triple bottom line” of profit, people, and planet. It proposes a systems dynamics framework to model how advertising can contribute to business innovation and profit within an equitable society and sustainable economy. Finally, the paper calls for research to investigate this positive future.

title: Ads that Talk Back: Implications and Perceptions of Injecting Personalized Advertising into LLM Chatbots
venue: Proceedings of the ACM on Interactive Mobile Wearable and Ubiquitous Technologies
authors: Brian Tang; Kaiwen Sun; Noah T. Curran; Florian Schaub; Kang Geun Shin
keywords: personalized advertising; large language models; chatbots; user preferences; AI in Service Interactions; Digital Marketing and Social Media; Information Retrieval and Search Behavior; cs.HC; cs.AI
queries: chatbot advertising user trust; LLM sponsored product recommendation; conversational agent advertising manipulation; personalized advertising AI privacy autonomy; advertising large language models
abstract: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have enabled the creation of highly effective chatbots. However, the compute costs of widely deploying LLMs have raised questions about profitability. Companies have proposed exploring ad-based revenue streams for monetizing LLMs, which could serve as the new de facto platform for advertising. This paper investigates the implications of personalizing LLM advertisements to individual users via a between-subjects experiment with 179 participants. We developed a chatbot that embeds personalized product advertisements within LLM responses, inspired by similar forays by AI companies. The evaluation of our benchmarks showed that ad injection only slightly impacted LLM performance, particularly response desirability. Results revealed that participants struggled to detect ads, and even preferred LLM responses with hidden advertisements. Rather than clicking on our advertising disclosure, participants tried changing their advertising settings using natural language queries. We created an advertising dataset and an open-source LLM, Phi-4-Ads, fine-tuned to serve ads and flexibly adapt to user preferences.

title: Real-time Ad Retrieval via LLM-generative Commercial Intention for Sponsored Search Advertising
venue: Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing (EMNLP)
authors: Tongtong Liu; Zhaohui Wang; Meiyue Qin; Zenghui Lu; Xudong Chen; Yuekui Yang; Peng Shu
keywords: search engine advertising; large language models; LLM-generated text; real-time retrieval; semantic representation; click-through rate; Information Retrieval and Search Behavior; Recommender Systems and Techniques; Topic Modeling
abstract: The integration of Large Language Models (LLMs) with retrieval systems has shown promising potential in retrieving documents (docs) or advertisements (ads) for a given query. Existing LLM-based retrieval methods generate numeric or content-based DocIDs to retrieve docs/ads. However, the one-to-few mapping between numeric IDs and docs, along with the time-consuming content extraction, leads to semantic inefficiency and limits the scalability of existing methods on large-scale corpora. In this paper, we propose the **R**eal-time **A**d **RE**trieval (RARE) framework, which leverages LLM-generated text called Commercial Intentions (CIs) as an intermediate semantic representation to directly retrieve ads for queries in real-time. These CIs are generated by a customized LLM injected with commercial knowledge, enhancing its domain relevance. Each CI corresponds to multiple ads, yielding a lightweight and scalable set of CIs. RARE has been implemented in a real-world online system, handling daily search volumes in billions. The online implementation has yielded significant benefits: a 5.04% increase in consumption, a 6.37% rise in Gross Merchandise Volume (GMV), a 1.28% enhancement in click-through rate (CTR) and a 5.29% increase in shallow conversions. Extensive offline experiments show RARE’s superiority over ten competitive baselines in four major categories.

title: Designing brand chatbots: The impact of chatbot’s personality on the user’s brand personality perception
authors: Soyeon Park
keywords: chatbots; brand personality; chatbot personality; customer service chatbots; chatbot prototype; consumer perception; AI in Service Interactions; Consumer Behavior in Brand Consumption and Identification; Social Robot Interaction and HRI
abstract:
Along with advancements in technologies, which include machine learning and artificial intelligence, chatbots are increasingly taking the place of employees that work as customer service agents and personal shoppers. Considering that the characteristics of employees can influence a consumer’s perception of brand personality (Aaker, 1997), this perception may also be affected by the chatbot’s personality. This paper aims to investigate the impact of a chatbot’s personality on a user’s perception of brand personality. 
 
Two brands, and their chatbots, are used as case studies. The empirical study comprises of two stages, in which the qualitative and the quantitative data are both gathered and analyzed. Firstly, an online survey was conducted to investigate the personalities of two existing brands and their respective chatbots. As a result, a gap in personality between one of the brands and its chatbot was identified. Next, two prototypes were built and then tested in the interview. One was the emulator of the current brand chatbot, and the other was a new chatbot designed to have a personality closer to the brand personality. 
 
The findings reveal that the chatbot’s personality may affect brand personality, even though the impact was smaller than expected because participants perceived that the two prototypes’ personalities were moderately close to the brand personality. Interestingly, interviewees revealed that the chatbot’s personality may have a greater influence if it is totally different from the brand personality. Based on the study findings, design considerations are suggested to help practitioners in designing brand chatbots.

title: Human vs. machine as message source in advertising: examining the persuasiveness of brand influencer type and the mediating role of source credibility for advertising effectiveness in social media advertising
authors: Weilu Zhang
keywords: social media influencers; AI agents; source credibility; advertising effectiveness; persuasion; social media advertising; influencer marketing; mediating effect; consumer behavior; AI-generated content; chatbots; Digital Marketing and Social Media; AI in Service Interactions; Marketing and Advertising Strategies
abstract: [EMBARGOED UNTIL 6/1/2023] Message source effects on persuasion of target audiences have been examined for decades by scholars in advertising, consumer behavior, communication, and psychology, among others. Myriads of studies are available on the subject, but in nearly every instance "source" is defined as a human and rarely is source defined as non-human, or machine. The rise of artificial intelligence (AI) as a message source urges scientific inquiry of the validity of those established theories in a new technology context. The focus of this dissertation is on that of the machine as source. By "machine" this study refers broadly to AI agents, defined to mean digitally created artificial beings that can think and perform tasks like a human. The specific AI agent examined here is that of SMIs, defined as AI agents who are associated with fame and perform human tasks using software and algorithms. The context of the study is social media, defined as "digital networked tools or technologies that enable communication, collaboration, and creative expression across social networks" (McMillan and Childers, 2017, p. 52). Influencer marketing is a crucial component of social media marketing, which is projected to become a $10 billion market by 2023 (Tan, 2019). The primary contribution of this study is, therefore, to understand SMIs' effectiveness in social media advertising. Considering that 95 percent of consumer interaction is projected to be powered by AI by the year of 2025 (Finance Digest, 2020), research to understand the impact of this transformation of message source (from human to machine) is urgently needed but rarely conducted to date. The most apparent machine sources, SMIs, are already being put to use in practice without fully understanding their effectiveness and risk, to replace human influencers. Human influencers, here, specifically refer to social media influencers (SMIs) "who have built a sizable social network of people following them and are seen as self-made microcelebrities" (Shan et al., 2020, p. 2). Indeed, this very notion is reflected in the warnings of the infamous physicist Stephen Hawking who predicted that, someday, machines may even replace humans. As much as this may sound like a futuristic movie, machines are beginning to replace humans in fields as far and wide as medicine, engineering, and transportation. For example, AI is cleaning floors at airports, taking people's temperatures, and even making salad in hospital dining-halls in response to the coronavirus pandemic (Semuels, 2020). In advertising, AI is taking over the work humans have traditionally done, from content matching to advertising creation (Rodgers, 2021). An SMI, Lil Miquela, even takes the spot that is usually reserved for a human and is named as one of Time's 25 most influential people on the internet in 2018 (Time, 2018). The proposed research is supported by survey results from consumers worldwide that paint a mixed picture --some consumers embrace AI for its potential benefits, whereas others fear that AI will hurt their privacy and ability to control their jobs, lives, and futures (Zhang and Dafoe, 2019), suggesting potential drawbacks of AI technology. This suggests that SMIs could trigger various perceptions among consumers that may lead to different outcomes. The challenge is to know the underlying psychological mechanisms to explain potential positive/negative outcomes, yet studies on the subject are rare but urgently needed. This dissertation investigates this phenomenon, specifically, potential benefits and drawbacks of using SMIs compared to (human) SMIs in social media advertising. Based on established theories of persuasion on advertising and brand endorsers, this dissertation identifies a crucial processing mechanism - source credibility - that is used to explain instances under which influencer type (i.e., AI vs. human) differentially influences advertising outcomes (i.e., attitude toward the advertisement, attitude toward brand, and purchase intentions). Source credibility is the source's truthfulness and believability perceived by the consumers (Roy et al., 2017). The treatment of source credibility as a mediating factor is a unique aspect of the research and that diverges from prior approaches that treat it as a predictor of persuasion. Rather, this research conceptualizes source credibility as dynamic, constantly changing, and not related in a simple way to the persuasiveness of an influencer type. Three dimensions of source credibility - expertise, trustworthiness, and physical attractiveness - are proposed to explain how an AI influencer may perform better/worse than a (human) SMI on advertising outcomes. A review of five decades' of source credibility studies noted several discrepancies regarding three dimensions of source credibility, suggesting gaps or unresolved issues in source credibility that deserve attention (see Pornpitakpan, 2004). Additionally, initial negative/positive dispositions toward the brand influencers, which has hardly been examined (see Pornpitakpan, 2004), will be measured in an effort to assess how much, if any, of a shift is detected in source credibility perceptions. To summarize, this research examines effectiveness of influencer type (artificial intelligence influencer vs. SMI) on persuasion of social media advertising (attitude toward the ad, attitude toward the brand, and purchase intentions). One mediator, source credibility, is proposed to explain the results. This is accomplished with a pilot study and an experimental study conducted in an online setting.

title: Proactive Hybrid Recommendation Advertising in Generative AI Text Dialogues: An AI-Initiated Text Advertising Format Integrating Organic and Sponsored Recommendations
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
authors: Jincheng Zhang
keywords: sponsorship disclosure; advertising ethics; AI in Service Interactions; Digital Marketing and Social Media; Recommender Systems and Techniques
queries: sponsored content conversational AI; native advertising generative AI; LLM sponsored product recommendation
abstract: The emergence of generative artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming digital communication by enabling users to obtain information, assistance, and recommendations through natural-language conversations. As generative AI platforms explore advertising-supported business models, an important research opportunity concerns the development of advertising formats that are native to text-based AI interactions rather than simply adapting conventional advertisements to conversational interfaces. This paper proposes Proactive Hybrid Text Advertising (PHTA), a conceptual advertising framework specifically designed for text-based generative AI dialogues. Under PHTA, a generative AI system proactively initiates and presents a unified textual recommendation list without waiting for the user to explicitly request product recommendations, service suggestions, or advertising content. The list integrates two distinct categories of recommendations: organic text recommendations, independently selected according to their relevance and potential usefulness to the user, and sponsored text recommendations, included through identifiable paid advertising arrangements. The defining contribution is the conceptualization of the entire AI-initiated hybrid recommendation list as an independent text advertising unit, rather than treating advertising exclusively as an isolated sponsored sentence, a paid recommendation appended to an ordinary AI response, or a sponsored entry within a user-requested recommendation list. The proposed framework introduces conversational-context analysis, proactive advertising-opportunity identification, organic recommendation generation, sponsored recommendation selection, hybrid-list construction, text-based sponsorship disclosure, and user-control mechanisms. It further establishes a separation between organic recommendation selection and advertiser-funded placement to reduce the risk that commercial incentives silently determine the AI system's independent recommendations. PHTA is designed to support contextual relevance, transparent commercial classification, conversational continuity, privacy protection, and user autonomy. This paper develops the conceptual foundations, architectural components, operational workflow, design requirements, evaluation propositions, and ethical considerations of the proposed format. It distinguishes the framework from existing research on conversational advertising, sponsored LLM responses, and proactive conversational AI by focusing on the combined mechanism of AI-initiated presentation and a unified organic–sponsored text recommendation list. No experimental results, validated performance improvements, or demonstrated commercial advantages are claimed. To the best of the author's knowledge, the specific combination and formalization of these mechanisms as a distinct proactive hybrid text advertising format for generative AI dialogues constitutes a research proposal warranting further systematic investigation.

title: Proactive Hybrid In-Stream Advertising in Generative AI Conversations: An AI-Initiated Advertising Architecture Integrating Organic Recommendations and Cross-Media Ad Inserts
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
authors: Jincheng Zhang
keywords: hybrid recommendation; conversational recommendation; user autonomy; contextual relevance; privacy; conversational continuity; Recommender Systems and Techniques; Digital Marketing and Social Media; AI in Service Interactions
abstract: This paper proposes Proactive Hybrid In-Stream Advertising (PHISA), a novel conceptual advertising architecture designed for generative artificial intelligence (AI) conversations. PHISA enables a generative AI system to proactively initiate a unified hybrid recommendation experience in which organically selected recommendations and commercially sponsored recommendations are integrated into a coherent presentation, with sponsored advertisements inserted within the recommendation sequence as in-stream advertising components. Unlike conventional advertising systems that primarily depend on users explicitly requesting recommendations, navigating advertising-supported content, or consuming independently selected media streams, PHISA allows the conversational AI system to initiate an advertising experience when contextual analysis identifies a potentially relevant recommendation opportunity. The user is not required to explicitly request recommendations or advertisements in the current conversational turn. A defining feature of the framework is that sponsored advertisements are not restricted to video. The proposed architecture accommodates cross-media in-stream advertising inserts, including text-based advertisements, image advertisements, audio advertisements, video advertisements, animations, rich-media advertisements, interactive advertisements, and other present or future advertising formats capable of being inserted into a content or recommendation sequence. These inserts may appear before, between, during, or after relevant recommendation segments, depending on the selected presentation configuration. Organic recommendations and sponsored recommendations are integrated into one coherent hybrid presentation, and the entire AI-initiated presentation constitutes a unified advertising unit rather than treating individual sponsored inserts as isolated advertisements. Each recommendation and advertising component nevertheless retains its own commercial provenance and disclosure status. To the best of the author's knowledge, PHISA is the first explicitly formulated conceptual framework to integrate proactive AI-initiated hybrid recommendations with cross-media in-stream advertising inserts as a unified advertising architecture specifically designed for generative AI conversations. This priority claim concerns the integrated architecture and its defining organizational principles, not the independent invention of advertising insertion, individual advertising formats, conversational recommendation, or generative AI advertising. The paper establishes the conceptual foundations, architecture, operational workflow, insertion configurations, design principles, research propositions, and evaluation methodology of PHISA. It further identifies essential requirements concerning commercial transparency, user autonomy, contextual relevance, privacy, and conversational continuity. As a conceptual contribution, this study provides a foundation for future technical implementation and empirical investigation without claiming experimentally demonstrated effectiveness.

title: The Dark Side of Generative AI in Marketing: AI-Generated False and Misleading Advertising and Its Consumer Consequences
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
authors: Pankaj Nandurkar; Pradeep Gupta; Sangram Andhe; Krishnakant Lasune
keywords: generative AI; AI hallucination; misleading advertising; perceived deception; AI skepticism; purchase intention; stimulus-organism-response model; consumer trust; AI-generated content; advertising transparency; AI in Service Interactions; Digital Marketing and Social Media; Marketing and Advertising Strategies
abstract: Abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is transforming advertising by enabling marketers to create persuasive text, images, and other promotional content rapidly and at lower cost. At the same time, the ability of generative systems to produce highly realistic content creates concerns about deception, misinformation, transparency, and the credibility of consumer-facing information. The present study examines the consumer consequences of AI-generated false and misleading advertising, with particular emphasis on hallucinated product claims. The study focuses on whether AI-generated hallucinated product claims influence perceived deception, AI skepticism, and perceived information reliability, and whether these consumer responses subsequently shape purchase intention. Drawing on the stimulus-organism-response (S-O-R) framework, the study conceptualizes hallucinated product claims as the stimulus, the three consumer evaluations as the organism, and purchase intention as the response. A quantitative, cross-sectional, deductive research design was adopted. Data were collected from 320 business-school students and faculty members through a structured questionnaire using a five-point Likert scale, and the model was assessed using SmartPLS. The reported measurement results show Cronbach's alpha values above 0.70, composite reliability above the stated threshold, and average variance extracted above 0.50 for all constructs, indicating acceptable reliability and convergent validity. The reported discriminant-validity matrix also supports construct distinctiveness. The structural model reports a VIF range of 1.47-2.24 and an R² of 0.421 for purchase intention. Four of the six hypotheses are supported. AI-generated hallucinated product claims significantly increase perceived deception and significantly reduce perceived information reliability. Perceived deception significantly reduces purchase intention, while perceived information reliability significantly increases purchase intention. The paths from hallucinated product claims to AI skepticism and from AI skepticism to purchase intention are not statistically significant. The findings indicate that message-level judgments of deception and information reliability are more consequential for purchase intention in the reported model than generalized skepticism toward AI. The study extends the S-O-R perspective to the dark side of GenAI in advertising and highlights the importance of factual verification, transparency, human oversight, disclosure, and consumer AI literacy. Keywords: Generative artificial intelligence; AI hallucinations; misleading advertising; perceived deception; AI skepticism; perceived information reliability; purchase intention; stimulus-organism-response theory.

title: Proactive Hybrid Recommendation Advertising: A Novel Advertising Format for Generative AI Based on AI-Initiated Lists of Organic and Sponsored Recommendations
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
authors: Jincheng Zhang
keywords: generative AI; conversational interfaces; recommendation transparency; advertising ethics; Recommender Systems and Techniques; Digital Marketing and Social Media; AI in Service Interactions
abstract: The emergence of generative artificial intelligence (AI) is creating new possibilities for integrating commercial communication into conversational interfaces. Conventional digital advertising typically relies on user-initiated searches, explicitly requested recommendations, advertisements embedded in content, or sponsored placements within established recommendation feeds. Generative AI introduces the possibility of a different advertising interaction in which the system independently identifies an appropriate opportunity during an ongoing conversation and proactively initiates a complete recommendation experience. This paper proposes Proactive Hybrid Recommendation Advertising (PHRA), a conceptual advertising framework in which a generative AI system proactively presents a unified recommendation list containing both organic recommendations and paid sponsored recommendations without waiting for the user to explicitly request product or service recommendations. The central contribution is the conceptualization of the entire AI-initiated hybrid recommendation list as a distinct advertising unit, rather than treating advertising as an isolated sponsored item appended to an otherwise organic recommendation response. Within this framework, organic recommendations are selected independently according to their relevance and potential value to the user, whereas sponsored recommendations are included through identifiable commercial arrangements with advertisers. Both categories appear within one coordinated recommendation presentation but remain transparently distinguishable in terms of commercial status, selection rationale, and sponsorship. The proposed architecture introduces conversational-context analysis, proactive opportunity identification, hybrid-list construction, organic and sponsored recommendation allocation, commercial disclosure, presentation management, and user-control mechanisms. It further establishes safeguards intended to prevent paid placement from silently determining organic recommendation quality or being misrepresented as an independent AI judgment. The framework distinguishes itself from conventional sponsored recommendation systems by combining AI-initiated presentation, unsolicited recommendation-list generation, and the integration of organic and sponsored recommendations into one unified advertising format. This paper develops the conceptual foundations, architectural components, operational workflow, design requirements, evaluation propositions, and ethical considerations of PHRA. It does not claim experimentally demonstrated effectiveness or verified commercial advantages. To the best of the author's knowledge, the specific combination of a proactively initiated, unified organic–sponsored recommendation list, conceptualized as an independent advertising format for generative AI conversations, represents a distinct architectural proposal that warrants further systematic investigation.

title: LLM-Auction: Generative Auction towards LLM-Native Advertising
authors: Zhao, Chujie; Hu, Qun; Song, Shiping; Dagui Chen; Zhu Han; Jian Xu; Zheng, Bo
keywords: online advertising; allocation mechanisms; preference alignment; mechanism design; LLM-as-a-judge; allocative efficiency; user experience; Auction Theory and Applications; Game Theory and Voting Systems; Recommender Systems and Techniques
queries: native advertising generative AI; LLM sponsored product recommendation
abstract: The commercialization of LLM applications is the next frontier in online advertising, with LLM-native advertising emerging as a promising paradigm by integrating ads into LLM-generated content. However, classic mechanisms are no longer applicable in this setting where the auction object is shifted from discrete ad slots to distributions over LLM outputs, and existing methods are impractical in industrial scenarios due to ignored externalities or high inference costs. To address these issues, we propose LLM-Auction, the first learning-based generative auction mechanism that integrates auction and generation. By formulating the allocation as preference alignment between LLM outputs and a mechanism objective that balances advertisers' value and user experience, we optimize the LLMs to inherently model allocation externalities without extra inference cost. Theoretically, we identify the allocation monotonicity and continuity of the optimal allocation rule of LLM-Auction, and prove that a simple first-price payment rule exhibits favorable incentive properties under this allocation rule. Furthermore, we build an LLM-as-a-judge simulation environment for quantitative evaluation, and experiments demonstrate that LLM-Auction achieves the state-of-the-art allocation efficiency while approximately satisfying key mechanism properties.

title: Effects of interaction between brand positioning and chatbot conversational style on perceived fit and brand attitudes
authors: Li Cheng; Chung‐Lin Toung
keywords: brand positioning; chatbots; conversational style; perceived fit; brand attitude; power states; human-chatbot interaction; brand associations; customer service automation; AI in Service Interactions; Consumer Behavior in Brand Consumption and Identification; Digital Marketing and Social Media
abstract: Although an underdog brand positioning can elicit positive consumer responses, maintaining a brand's positioning requires maintaining consistent brand associations. If the associations created by the company's service providers do not align with the brand's positioning, this discrepancy can lead to consumer confusion or to a decline in brand attitudes. Chatbots, as customer‐facing representatives, play a crucial role in how consumers perceive and evaluate a brand. However, the role of chatbots in shaping brand attitude has not been extensively studied. Therefore, this study investigates the effects of chatbot conversational styles on consumers' perceptions of the fit between a brand's positioning and its messaging, focusing on both “top‐dog” and “underdog” brands. This study demonstrates that underdog brands using chatbots with warm conversational styles and top‐dog brands using chatbots with competent (i.e., professional) conversational styles foster positive brand evaluations by consumers through perceived fit. Additionally, this study introduces the concept of power state—an individual's degree of perceived control over their surroundings—as a moderator in human–chatbot interactions, demonstrating that high‐power‐state consumers of top‐dog brands favor a competent conversational style, whereas low‐power‐state consumers favor a warm conversational style regardless of the brand's positioning.

title: When AI Conversations Become Advertising Data: Algorithmic Trust, Privacy Calculus, and Purchase Intention in GenAI-Personalized Social Commerce
venue: Journal of theoretical and applied electronic commerce research
authors: Omar Munther Nusir; Che Aniza Che Wel; Siti Ngayesah Ab Hamid
keywords: generative AI assistants; personalized advertising; social commerce; algorithmic trust; privacy concerns; purchase intention; privacy calculus; trust theory; stimulus-organism-response model; AI in Service Interactions; Privacy, Security, and Data Protection; Digital Marketing and Social Media
abstract: This study examines how consumers respond to personalized advertisements that appear to be derived from prior conversations with generative AI assistants in social commerce settings. Drawing on the Privacy Calculus Theory, Trust Theory, and the Stimulus–Organism–Response framework, the study investigates whether perceived GenAI-based advertising personalization simultaneously creates perceived personalization value and privacy concerns, and how these evaluations shape algorithmic trust and social commerce purchase intention. A scenario-based survey was conducted with 435 social commerce users in Jordan. Respondents evaluated a situation in which a product advertisement appeared to reflect a previous conversation with a generative AI assistant. The data were analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling with SmartPLS 4. The findings show that perceived GenAI-based advertising personalization increases both perceived personalization value and privacy concerns. Personalization value strengthens algorithmic trust, whereas privacy concerns weaken it. Algorithmic trust, in turn, strongly enhances social commerce purchase intention. The mediation results show that personalization value and privacy concerns transmit the dual effect of perceived GenAI-based advertising personalization to algorithmic trust. In contrast, algorithmic trust transmits these effects to purchase intention. Perceived transparency disclosure does not significantly reduce privacy concerns, but it strengthens the positive relationship between personalization value and algorithmic trust. This study contributes to digital marketing and social commerce research by showing that GenAI-personalized advertising can be perceived as both useful and intrusive and that perceived transparency disclosure may support trust formation without necessarily eliminating privacy concerns.

title: Commercialized Generative AI: A Critical Study of the Feasibility and Ethics of Generating Native Advertising Using Large Language Models in Conversational Web Search
authors: Ines Zelch; Matthias Hagen; Martin Potthast
keywords: large language models; native advertising; search engine results; brand placement; advertising disclosure; organic search; AI ethics; advertising ethics; Information Retrieval and Search Behavior; Ethics and Social Impacts of AI; Digital Marketing and Social Media; cs.IR
queries: advertising large language models; native advertising generative AI
abstract: How will generative AI pay for itself? Unless charging users for access, selling advertising is the only alternative. Especially in the multi-billion dollar web search market with ads as the main source of revenue, the introduction of a subscription model seems unlikely. The recent disruption of search by generative large language models could thus ultimately be accompanied by generated ads. Our concern is that the commercialization of generative AI in general and large language models in particular could lead to native advertising in the form of quite subtle brand or product placements. In web search, the evolution of search engine results pages (SERPs) from traditional lists of ``ten blue links'' (lists SERPs) to generated text with web page references (text SERPs) may further blur the line between advertising-based and organic search results, making it difficult for users to distinguish between the two, depending on how advertising is integrated and disclosed. To raise awareness of this potential development, we conduct a pilot study analyzing the capabilities of current large language models to blend ads with organic search results. Although the models still struggle to subtly frame ads in an unrelated context, their potential is evident when integrating ads into related topics which calls for further investigation.

title: Generative AI Disclosure in Fashion Marketing: A Tectonic Shift in the Advertising Landscape
authors: Hyunjeong Rhee; Kyu‐Hye Lee
keywords: generative AI; AI-generated advertising; disclosure; fashion marketing; consumer perception; affective states; brand attitude; perceived effort; risk perception; AI in Service Interactions; Digital Marketing and Social Media; Consumer Behavior in Brand Consumption and Identification
abstract: The advent of generative artificial intelligence (AI) has leveraged fashion marketing by enabling swift and efficient content creation. However, a research gap in understanding its acceptance from the perspective of a consumer viewing an AI-generated advertisement remains, while regulations begin to make disclosure mandatory. As generative AI is envisioned to bring immense innovation to marketing methods, a between-subject experimental study was developed to test the effects of AI-generated advertisement disclosure on consumer affective states and thus motivational outcomes. Evidence shows that while negative perception regarding AI-generated content was prevalent, perceived effort and brand attitude hold potential to alleviate the detrimental effects of AI-generated image disclosure, without provoking consumers’ perceived risk. Findings show managerial implications for the future of AI-generated content in fashion marketing.

title: Dimensional Collapse in AI-Mediated Search: Large Language Models as Metameric Observers of Brand Advertising
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
authors: Dmitry Zharnikov
keywords: large language models; brand advertising; brand perception; dimensional collapse; search engine advertising; agentic commerce; brand differentiation; cross-cultural advertising; geopolitical context; Consumer Behavior in Brand Consumption and Identification; Digital Marketing and Social Media; Information Retrieval and Search Behavior
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly mediate consumer brand evaluation in search and agentic commerce. This study demonstrates that LLMs systematically collapse brand perception to Experiential and Economic dimensions, leaving brands differentiated on narrative, ideological, cultural, or temporal dimensions metameric by inference, not by measured inter-brand distance. Using PRISM-B across 21,350 API calls to 24 models spanning seven training traditions and 15 languages, a Dimensional Collapse Index (DCI; uniform baseline = .250) is computed. Mean DCI equals .294 for global brands (p < .001) and .356 cross-culturally (d = 3.373). Cross-model convergence is near-perfect (cosine = .977). Local brands collapse 20% more severely than global brands (d = .92, in five FMCG pairs tested). Native-language prompting is null in home markets (p = .716) but reduces collapse up to .095 in foreign-market frames (p = .002). Geopolitical context independently modulates weights (p < .001). Structured Brand Function specifications remove two-thirds of above-baseline excess (.103 to .034). Collapse is stable across model versions. For search advertising, these findings reframe strategy from platform selection to dimensional defensibility: advertisers must encode soft brand dimensions in verifiable, machine-readable form or risk erasure by LLM intermediaries. Patterns reflect the text-conditioned LLM observers tested here. Includes zharnikov-2026v-ai-search-metamerism.yaml (Paper Spec v0.1.0) – a machine-readable specification of the paper’s claims, assumptions, and dependencies. The paper’s full machine-first bundle (the SPINE claim/dependency graph and the ONTOLOGY term module) lives in the public repository; see github.com/spectralbranding/paper-spec for the standard. This PDF is generated programmatically from that machine-first source under a research-as-repository model.

title: The Effects of Generative AI Advertising Disclosure on Brand Authenticity Perceptions Purchase Intention and Consumer Skepticism Among Generation Z Consumers
venue: International Journal of Scientific Research in Humanities and Social Sciences
authors: Samuel Bradley Doe Gadekah; Joy Onma Enyejo
keywords: AI disclosure; brand authenticity; purchase intention; consumer skepticism; Generation Z consumers; advertising credibility; AI familiarity; perceived transparency; AI literacy; brand familiarity; consumer trust; Consumer Behavior in Brand Consumption and Identification; AI in Service Interactions; Digital Marketing and Social Media
abstract: The increasing application of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in digital advertising has introduced substantial changes in how brands develop promotional content, communicate product information, and establish relationships with consumers. However, explicitly disclosing AI involvement in advertisement production may influence perceived brand authenticity, purchase intention, and consumer skepticism, particularly among Generation Z consumers who demonstrate considerable familiarity with digitally mediated brand communication. This study proposes an integrated computational and behavioural framework for investigating the direct, indirect, and conditional effects of generative AI advertising disclosure on consumer responses. A novel Disclosure–Authenticity–Skepticism Predictive Model (DASPM) is developed to quantify how disclosure characteristics, including disclosure visibility, specificity, timing, and perceived transparency, influence brand authenticity perceptions and purchase intention through consumer skepticism. The proposed framework integrates structural equation modelling (SEM), moderated mediation analysis, and machine learning techniques to examine both theoretically specified causal pathways and complex predictive relationships. A randomized experimental survey involving Generation Z consumers aged 18–29 years is proposed, using matched advertisements assigned to three conditions: undisclosed AI-generated advertising, explicitly disclosed AI-generated advertising, and human-created advertising. Brand authenticity, consumer skepticism, advertising credibility, AI familiarity, and purchase intention are measured using validated multi-item Likert scales. The DASPM framework incorporates latent-variable estimation, interaction effects, nonlinear feature transformations, and predictive modelling, with its performance evaluated against conventional multiple linear regression, partial least squares structural equation modelling (PLS-SEM), Random Forest, and Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost). Comparative evaluation will employ coefficient of determination (R²), root mean squared error (RMSE), mean absolute error (MAE), and cross-validated predictive performance, alongside bootstrapped indirect-effect estimates and measurement validity assessments. The results section is designed to present comparative performance graphs, conditional indirect-effect plots, disclosure-treatment comparisons, and feature-importance analyses to determine whether transparent AI disclosure strengthens consumer trust or activates skepticism that reduces purchase intention. The study will also investigate whether perceived brand authenticity mediates the disclosure–purchase intention relationship and whether AI literacy and prior brand familiarity moderate these effects. The proposed framework is intended to advance understanding of generative AI advertising disclosure by combining experimental consumer research with interpretable predictive analytics, providing an evidence-based approach to evaluating disclosure strategies and their implications for brand communication among Generation Z consumers.

title: Persuasiveness of Conversational Agents for Targeted Advertising: Autism and Gen-AI Chatbots
venue: Proceedings of the ACM on Human-Computer Interaction
authors: Kirsten Chapman; Kaitlyn Klabacka; Garrett Smith; Xinru Page
keywords: generative AI chatbots; targeted advertising; persuasive technology; autism spectrum disorder; young adults with autism; consumer preference change; anthropomorphism; financial literacy; AI in Service Interactions; Social Robot Interaction and HRI; Digital Marketing and Social Media
abstract: Marketing firms are starting to leverage Generative-AI-based chatbots as a more persuasive form of advertising. This is potentially more harmful for autistic young adults with substantial support needs who tend to have lower financial literacy, be more trusting of bad actors when communicating through social technologies, and more likely to anthropomorphize objects. Thus, we investigated whether a chatbot assuming the likeness of a favorite celebrity would more greatly influence consumer preferences of this population when compared against either autistic individuals without substantial support needs or the general population. We conducted an experimental survey where participants 1) ranked their preferences of various consumer items, 2) performed intervening tasks answering several questions, 3) viewed a chatbot interaction where the chatbot exhibited opposite consumer preferences, and then 4) re-ranked their preferences for those items. We found that autistic young adults with substantial support needs were more likely to change their preferences than the sample from the general population. Moreover, they were also more likely to change their preferences than autistic young adults without substantial support needs. These findings suggest that autistic individuals with substantial support needs are more susceptible to celebrity chatbot persuasion. We discuss the risks and guardrails that need to be associated with deploying generative-AI-based chatbots for targeted advertising.

title: The Impact of AI-Generated Advertising on Consumer Trust and Brand Credibility
venue: Journal of Business Insight and Innovation
authors: Amjid Khan; Shahzad Afzal Kiyani; Imran Muhammad; Raheem Ullah; Alvina Khan
keywords: AI-generated advertising; consumer trust; brand credibility; advertising quality; transparency; authenticity; source credibility; persuasion knowledge model; AI in Service Interactions; Digital Marketing and Social Media; Marketing and Advertising Strategies
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) can be leveraged to create advertising text, graphics, videos, virtual representatives, product descriptions and personalized advertisements. While these applications can boost production efficiency and support quick experimentation, they also pose key challenges regarding authenticity, transparency, consumer trust, and brand credibility. The present study aims to explore the connections of the quality, transparency, authenticity, consumer trust and brand credibility with the perceived advertising quality of AI-generated advertisements in Pakistan. Based on the theories of source credibility, the Persuasion Knowledge Model and trust and signalling, a conceptual model is formulated for further exploration. A quantitative, cross-sectional, correlational research design is used, and all five constructs are measured by five-point Likert scales. Descriptive statistics, Cronbach's alpha, Pearson correlation, and multiple regression are used in the analysis. The analysis results showed good internal consistency for each of the five constructs, ranging from .826 to .853 for Cronbach's alpha coefficient. Together, the three-advertising quality, transparency, and authenticity explain 38.5% of the variance in consumer trust. In addition, although consumer trust, advertising quality, and advertising authenticity show statistically significant positive relationship with brand credibility, transparency does not make a unique contribution after the other predictors are taken into account. The results underscore the need to consider relationships between the characteristics of AI-generated ads and the evaluations of their consumers. The study highlights the importance of transparent communication and the need for factual accuracy, human oversight, and verified advertising claims in responsible AI-driven marketing. The relationships between disclosure of AI and consumer trust and brand credibility should be explored with validated measurement instruments, systematic sampling, and experimental designs for future research to determine the relationship between the two. title: Proactive Hybrid Advertising (PHA): A Conceptual Framework for AI-Initiated Integration of Organic and Sponsored Content in Generative AI
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
authors: Jincheng Zhang
keywords: sponsored content; organic matter content; native advertising; advertising disclosure; user autonomy; content integrity; contextual relevance; Digital Marketing and Social Media; Marketing and Advertising Strategies; AI in Service Interactions
queries: sponsored content conversational AI; native advertising generative AI
abstract: This paper introduces Proactive Hybrid Advertising (PHA), a conceptual advertising framework for generative artificial intelligence (AI) that establishes an AI-initiated approach to integrating organic content and advertiser-sponsored content within the same AI-generated output. Unlike conventional advertising approaches that predominantly depend on explicit user requests, search activities, content consumption, or separately designated advertising placements, PHA enables a generative AI system to proactively initiate an advertising opportunity and incorporate commercially sponsored content into its generated response without requiring the user to explicitly request advertising or recommendations in the current conversational turn. The defining principle is the coexistence of two fundamentally distinguishable content categories within a unified generative output: organic content, which is generated or selected independently of payment-based placement according to contextual relevance and potential user usefulness, and sponsored content, whose inclusion or presentation is supported by an advertiser's commercial arrangement. The commercial origin of sponsored content must remain transparently identifiable, even when it is naturally integrated into the surrounding generated content. Crucially, PHA does not prescribe a particular response structure, advertising placement, media format, or presentation mechanism. Its architecture is independent of whether the generated output takes the form of continuous prose, dialogue, explanations, recommendations, narratives, multimedia responses, or other forms of generative expression. Nor does it require organic and sponsored content to occupy separate, predefined sections. Instead, PHA establishes a general principle of proactive hybrid content generation in which organic and sponsored content can coexist within the same AI-generated output while retaining distinguishable commercial provenance. The framework identifies three defining characteristics: proactive AI initiation, hybrid integration of organic and sponsored content, and presentation-format independence. To the best of the author's knowledge, this paper presents the world's first explicitly formulated conceptual framework that defines these three characteristics together as a unified advertising paradigm for generative AI. This priority claim concerns the specific integrated conceptual framework rather than the independent invention of conversational advertising, sponsored content, native advertising, or proactive conversational systems. The paper establishes the conceptual foundations, formal definition, theoretical positioning, design principles, research propositions, and evaluation directions of PHA. It further emphasizes that commercial transparency, user autonomy, content integrity, and contextual relevance are essential conditions for responsible implementation.
