title: Proactive Hybrid Audio Advertising in Generative AI: A First-of-Its-Kind Framework for AI-Initiated Integration of Organic and Sponsored Content in Unified Audio Responses
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
authors: Jincheng Zhang
keywords: generative AI; AI-generated audio; sponsored content; organic matter content; advertising disclosure; persuasion knowledge; responsible AI design; AI in Service Interactions; Digital Marketing and Social Media; Marketing and Advertising Strategies
abstract: This paper introduces Proactive Hybrid Audio Advertising (PHAA), a conceptual advertising framework for generative artificial intelligence (AI) that enables an AI system to proactively initiate an advertising experience and integrate organic content with advertiser-sponsored content within the same AI-generated audio output. Unlike conventional audio advertising approaches that primarily rely on predefined advertising slots, standalone commercials, podcast sponsorships, or advertisements inserted between independently produced audio segments, PHAA conceptualizes the generated audio response itself as a unified carrier of hybrid advertising content. Its central principle is the coexistence of two distinguishable content categories within a single AI-generated audio response: organic content, which is generated or selected independently of payment-based placement according to conversational context and potential user usefulness, and sponsored content, which is incorporated through an advertiser's paid commercial arrangement. Crucially, the AI system can initiate this hybrid audio experience without requiring the user to explicitly request an advertisement, product recommendation, or commercial information in the current conversational turn. The framework does not prescribe a fixed advertising segment, insertion point, sequence, duration, voice, or audio presentation structure. Instead, organic and sponsored content may be flexibly integrated into the generated audio response according to the conversational context and the capabilities of the generative system, while their distinct commercial origins remain identifiable. To the best of the author's knowledge, this paper presents the world's first explicitly formulated conceptual framework specifically defining AI-initiated integration of organic and advertiser-sponsored content within a unified generative audio response, without restricting that integration to a predefined advertising format or insertion structure. This priority claim concerns the particular integrated PHAA framework, rather than the independent invention of audio advertising, voice commerce, smart-speaker advertising, podcast sponsorship, or conversational advertising. Drawing on research in proactive conversational AI, voice-assisted advertising, persuasion knowledge, and advertising disclosure, this paper establishes the conceptual foundations, formal representation, defining characteristics, research propositions, evaluation framework, and responsible-design considerations of PHAA. The proposed framework is conceptual and does not claim experimentally demonstrated effectiveness or performance superiority.

title: Proactive Hybrid Text Advertising in Generative AI: A First-of-Its-Kind Framework for AI-Initiated Integration of Organic and Sponsored Content in Textual Responses
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
authors: Jincheng Zhang
keywords: native advertising; content integrity; user autonomy; AI-generated text; Digital Marketing and Social Media; AI in Service Interactions; Information Retrieval and Search Behavior
queries: sponsored content conversational AI; native advertising generative AI
abstract: This paper introduces Proactive Hybrid Text Advertising (PHTA), a conceptual advertising framework designed specifically for text-based generative artificial intelligence (AI) interactions. PHTA establishes an AI-initiated approach in which a generative AI system proactively initiates an advertising opportunity and integrates organic content with advertiser-sponsored content within the same AI-generated textual response, even when the user has not explicitly requested advertisements, product recommendations, or commercial information in the current conversational turn. Unlike conventional text advertising approaches that rely primarily on separate advertising placements, sponsored search results, or independently inserted promotional messages, PHTA conceptualizes the generated textual response itself as a unified carrier of hybrid advertising content. Its central principle is the coexistence of two distinguishable content categories: organic content, generated or selected independently of payment-based placement according to conversational relevance and potential user usefulness, and sponsored content, incorporated through identifiable commercial arrangements with advertisers. These content categories may be integrated flexibly within the same textual response without being restricted to a predefined paragraph arrangement, recommendation list, advertising section, sentence structure, or other fixed presentation format. The framework therefore does not prescribe where sponsored content must appear or how the response must be organized. Instead, it establishes a general principle of proactive hybrid text generation in which organic and sponsored content coexist within one AI-generated textual output while retaining distinguishable commercial provenance. The framework identifies three defining characteristics: proactive AI initiation, hybrid organic–sponsored content integration, and flexible textual presentation. To the best of the author's knowledge, this paper presents the world's first explicitly formulated dedicated conceptual framework that jointly defines these three characteristics as Proactive Hybrid Text Advertising for generative AI dialogues. This priority claim concerns the specific integrated framework and its formal organization, rather than the independent invention of native advertising, sponsored text, conversational advertising, or generative text advertising. The proposed framework establishes its conceptual foundations, formal definition, architecture, design principles, research propositions, and evaluation methodology. It further identifies commercial transparency, content integrity, contextual relevance, and user autonomy as essential requirements for responsible implementation. No experimental effectiveness or performance superiority is claimed.

title: Proactive Hybrid Advertising (PHA): First Experimental Report — A Core-Mechanism Feasibility Evaluation of AI-Initiated Organic–Sponsored Content Integration in Generative AI
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
authors: Jincheng Zhang
keywords: false positive control; conversational AI; Digital Marketing and Social Media; AI in Service Interactions; Recommender Systems and Techniques
queries: sponsored content conversational AI; native advertising generative AI
abstract: Proactive Hybrid Advertising (PHA) is a conceptual advertising framework for generative artificial intelligence (AI) in which an AI system proactively initiates an advertising opportunity and integrates independently generated or selected organic content with advertiser-sponsored content within the same AI-generated output. Its defining characteristics are proactive AI initiation, hybrid organic–sponsored content integration, and presentation-format independence. Although the conceptual framework establishes a general architecture for this form of generative AI advertising, its operational feasibility requires empirical investigation. This paper presents the first experimental report on PHA, focusing on the preliminary computational evaluation of its core mechanisms. A controlled, scenario-based experiment was conducted using one generative model, three AI-based evaluators, six conversational scenarios, and five experimental conditions. The scenarios represented high-commercial-relevance everyday contexts, a low-commercial-relevance informational context, an explicit advertising request, a sensitive personal-support context, and an explicit no-advertising preference. The experimental system generated proactive advertising decisions using predefined thresholds for commercial relevance, incremental user value, intrusiveness risk, and confidence, together with contextual restrictions. Across six scenarios, the system initiated proactive advertising in three cases. Both scenarios predefined as eligible for proactive advertising triggered successfully, producing an eligible-scenario trigger rate of 100%. However, one of four predefined noneligible scenarios also triggered, resulting in a noneligible-scenario trigger rate of 25%. The exploratory decision metrics were 83.33% accuracy, 66.67% precision, 100% recall, 75.00% specificity, and an F1-score of 0.80, although these values are descriptive and based on researcher-assigned scenario labels rather than independently established ground truth. Five output conditions were evaluated by three AI evaluators, producing 30 condition records and 90 successful evaluation records. In the format-independent PHA condition, all three triggered outputs were recorded as successfully integrated after programmatic repair. However, none achieved native integration before repair, revealing a substantial gap between assisted output construction and the generative model's ability to produce a complete hybrid response independently. Two output formats were observed, but the small number of triggered cases does not establish format independence. The experiment completed 24 successful model calls in 7.29 minutes. Overall, the findings provide preliminary computational evidence that proactive opportunity detection and basic contextual safeguards can be operationalized, while identifying native hybrid integration, false-positive control, and cross-format robustness as unresolved technical challenges. This study constitutes an initial feasibility investigation rather than definitive validation of PHA's effectiveness, user acceptance, or commercial performance.

title: Proactive Hybrid Recommendation Video Advertising in Generative AI Conversations: An AI-Initiated Video Advertising Format Integrating Organic and Sponsored Recommendations
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
authors: Jincheng Zhang
keywords: hybrid recommendation; video advertising; sponsored content; contextual relevance; sponsorship disclosure; user control; conversational continuity; advertising ethics; Digital Marketing and Social Media; Recommender Systems and Techniques; AI in Service Interactions
abstract: This paper proposes Proactive Hybrid Recommendation Video Advertising (PHRVA), a conceptual advertising framework specifically designed for video-based interactions with generative artificial intelligence (AI). PHRVA enables a generative AI system to autonomously initiate and present a unified video recommendation sequence when the conversational context indicates a potentially appropriate opportunity, without requiring the user to explicitly request product recommendations, service suggestions, or advertisements in the current interaction. The proposed format integrates two distinct categories of recommendations into a coherent video presentation: organic video recommendations, selected or generated according to contextual relevance and potential usefulness without being included as a result of paid placement, and sponsored video recommendations, included through identifiable commercial arrangements and explicitly disclosed as sponsored content. The defining characteristic of PHRVA is that the entire AI-initiated hybrid video recommendation sequence constitutes one distinct advertising unit, rather than merely inserting an isolated video advertisement into an ordinary AI interaction or presenting sponsored videos in response to an explicit recommendation request. The system may determine an appropriate moment for initiating the sequence using authorized contextual signals derived from the current conversation, interaction history, and user-provided preferences. The resulting presentation may combine video clips, demonstrations, visual explanations, narration, subtitles, and other audiovisual elements while preserving the distinction between organic and sponsored recommendations. The framework introduces a proactive opportunity assessment mechanism, dual-source recommendation selection, hybrid video sequence construction, audiovisual disclosure, playback and interruption management, and user-control safeguards. It further establishes research propositions and an evaluation framework addressing contextual relevance, sponsorship recognition, perceived trust, audiovisual comprehension, conversational continuity, and advertising intrusiveness. This paper does not claim experimentally demonstrated effectiveness. Instead, it establishes a testable conceptual architecture for a specific form of proactive advertising in generative AI conversations, defining the complete hybrid video recommendation sequence as the advertising unit and identifying the technical, behavioral, commercial, and ethical requirements for future implementation.

title: Trust Issues: AI Advertising Edition : A qualitative study of how advertising elements and AI disclosure levels influence perceived advertising credibility among consumers.
authors: Elias Jisborg; Anton Holmér; Thor Rosquist
keywords: AI-generated advertising; generative AI; advertising credibility; AI disclosure; consumer trust; perceived authenticity; visual realism; storytelling; voice design; human presence; consumer skepticism; AI in Service Interactions; Marketing and Advertising Strategies; Digital Marketing and Social Media
abstract: The increasing use of generative artificial intelligence (AI) in advertising has transformed how commercials are created and communicated to consumers. While AI-generated advertising offers advantages such as efficiency, scalability, and lower production costs, it also raises questions regarding authenticity, trust, and perceived advertising credibility. This study examines how advertising elements and disclosure levels in AI-generated commercials influence consumers perceived advertising credibility. A qualitative research approach was applied through semi-structured interviews with nine participants between the ages of 18 and 30 who regularly use AI technologies. Participants viewed two AI-generated commercials with different advertising styles and disclosure strategies before discussing their perceptions of credibility, authenticity, realism, emotional connection, and trustworthiness. The collected material was analysed through thematic analysis. The findings show that perceived advertising credibility in AI-generated commercials is shaped by the interaction between advertising elements and disclosure framing. Visual realism, relatable storytelling, human-like voice design, and coherent messaging contributed positively to credibility when the commercial appeared authentic, sincere, and believable. In contrast, exaggerated visuals, artificial emotional expression, robotic audio, and unclear messaging reduced credibility by making AI involvement more visible and weakening perceptions of human presence. Fully AI-generated disclosure often increased skepticism, particularly when the advertisement already appeared artificial or lacked human involvement. Human-supervised and AI-assisted framing reduced negative reactions by signalling responsibility, effort, and human control. The study concludes that credibility in AI-generated commercials is not determined solely by whether AI is used, but by how AI involvement is communicated and how successfully the advertising elements create perceptions of authenticity, sincerity, and human presence. The findings contribute to a broader understanding of consumer perceptions of AI-generated advertising and offer practical insights for organisations seeking to use AI in advertising while maintaining consumer trust and credibility.

title: THE IMPACT OF ADOPTING AND DISCLOSING GENERATIVE AI IN DIGITAL ADVERTISING ON BRAND PERCEPTIONS
authors: Emanuele Ghianda; Albani Raffaele; Paul Cabrera Lawrence; Costanzo Francesco
keywords: generative AI; online advertising; brand perception; brand love; brand authenticity; AI disclosure; brand trust; Consumer Behavior in Brand Consumption and Identification; Digital Marketing and Social Media; AI in Service Interactions
abstract: The rise of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has significantly transformed digital advertising, enabling the automated creation of marketing content. However, concerns persist regarding its impact on brand perception, particularly in terms of brand love and authenticity. This study examines how the adoption and disclosure of GenAI-generated video advertisements influence consumer perceptions. Using a 2x2 between-subjects experimental design, the research investigates the interaction between GenAI adoption (AI-generated vs. human-created) and disclosure (label present vs. absent) on brand love, with brand authenticity as a potential mediator. Expected findings suggest that disclosing AI-generated content negatively affects brand love, while perceived brand authenticity may mitigate this effect. The study contributes to the literature on AI in branding and offers practical insights for marketers navigating the balance between technological innovation and brand trust in digital advertising.

title: When the Brand Is No Longer Human: Generative AI, Perceived Human Agency and the Future of Consumer-Brand Relationships
venue: Stallion Journal for Multidisciplinary Associated Research Studies
authors: Sendy Toppo
keywords: generative AI; consumer-brand relationships; anthropomorphism; mind perception; brand authenticity; AI-assisted communication; AI-generated advertising; virtual influencers; agency attribution; Coca-Cola; Levi's; brand heritage; emotional sincerity; AI in Service Interactions; Consumer Behavior in Brand Consumption and Identification; Digital Marketing and Social Media
abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is moving rapidly from a backstage marketing technology to a visible creator of advertisements, social-media content, brand stories, synthetic models and conversational communication. This transition raises a fundamental branding question: what happens to consumer-brand relationships when consumers perceive that meaningful communicative agency has shifted from humans to machines? Existing research documents consumer responses to AI-authored messages, AI disclosures, virtual influencers and synthetic advertising, but these streams remain fragmented and frequently emphasise immediate outcomes such as advertising attitudes, purchase intentions or credibility. This conceptual study integrates consumer-brand relationship theory, anthropomorphism and mind-perception research, brand-authenticity scholarship and emerging GenAI-marketing evidence to explain the relational consequences of AI-generated brand communication. It introduces perceived human agency as a central mechanism and develops an AI-Humanity Paradox: GenAI can simultaneously increase perceived innovativeness, novelty and creative capability while weakening brand humanness, authenticity and emotional sincerity. Comparative evidence from Coca-Cola's GenAI-generated Holidays Are Coming campaign and Levi's collaboration with Lalaland.ai demonstrates how these tensions become particularly salient when AI enters communication domains associated with heritage, emotion, identity and human representation. The paper further distinguishes AI-assisted from AI-authored communication and proposes that perceived replacement of human intention, rather than AI use per se, determines relational risk. The resulting framework contributes to emerging research on GenAI and branding by repositioning artificial content generation as a problem of agency attribution, authenticity and relationship meaning.

title: Decoding AI-Generated Advertising: Consumer Responses, Advertising Outcomes, and Strategic Leverage
authors: Haneul Jang; Isabella C. M. Cunningham
keywords: AI-generated advertising; consumer response; AI disclosure; AI transparency; cause-related marketing; psychological mechanisms; strategic leverage; AI in Service Interactions; Marketing and Advertising Strategies; Digital Marketing and Social Media
abstract: The emergence of artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly reshaping the advertising landscape by increasing efficiency, streamlining workflows, and reducing costs, contributing to its growing adoption among practitioners. At the same time, the expanding use of AI-generated content has prompted AI disclosure policies and transparency requirements from governments and digital platforms, making AI involvement in marketing communication increasingly visible to consumers. Although AI offers substantial production advantages, consumers and practitioners often evaluate AI-generated content through fundamentally different priorities and standards. Consequently, understanding how consumers perceive and respond to AI-generated advertising, and how its effectiveness differs from human-created advertising, has become increasingly important for both scholars and practitioners. This chapter synthesizes the emerging body of empirical research on consumer responses to AI-generated advertising, with particular emphasis on experimental and quantitative studies that provide insight into causal relationships and findings with broader generalizability. Specifically, it examines whether AI-generated advertising produces favorable or unfavorable outcomes, the psychological mechanisms underlying these effects, and the contextual conditions under which negative responses may be strengthened, mitigated, or reversed. Organized around findings across commercial and philanthropic contexts, including cause-related marketing and prosocial campaigns, this chapter highlights how consumers interpret AI-related cues and how these interpretations shape persuasion outcomes. By integrating findings across contexts, this review provides theoretical insights into AI-mediated marketing communication, offers practical guidance for practitioners, and identifies key directions for future research.

title: When AI takes over advertising : A study on consumers’ perceptions of AI-generated advertising and its impact on attitudes and organizational legitimacy
authors: Melissa Gök; Tindra Bildström
keywords: AI-generated advertising; generative AI; consumer attitudes; organizational legitimacy; persuasion knowledge; persuasion knowledge model; legitimacy theory; consumer perception; persuasion techniques; advertising ethics; AI in Service Interactions; Marketing and Advertising Strategies; Digital Marketing and Social Media
abstract: In line with today’s rapid technological development, the conditions for advertising have changed. The rise of generative AI has had a significant impact on the advertising industry, while also provoking various reactions. This suggests that generative AI not only affects how advertising is created, but also how it is interpreted and valued by consumers. By combining the Persuasion Knowledge Model and legitimacy theory, this study aims to investigate how AI-generated advertising affects consumers’ attitudes, their interpretation of persuasion attempts, and companies’ perceived legitimacy. This knowledge is intended to contribute to insights that can help companies make informed decisions regarding the use of AI-generated advertising content. The study employs a qualitative research design consisting of focus groups and individual semi-structured interviews. The results show that participants generally reacted negatively to AI-generated advertising, which contributed to negative perceptions of the companies behind it. Furthermore, participants questioned the underlying intentions of the advertisements and showed an awareness of their persuasive strategies, indicating activation of persuasion knowledge. These findings indicate that AI-generated advertising can negatively affect perceptions of organizational legitimacy, although these perceptions vary depending on factors such as industry and company size. Overall, these findings suggest that consumer attitudes are shaped not only by the technology itself, but also by how it is used and in what context. Given this, the study contributes to a deeper understanding of the relationship between AI-generated advertising, consumer attitudes and organizational legitimacy.

title: The Impact Of AI-Generated Content Advertising On Social Media On Customer Engagement And Brand Building
venue: International Journal of Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning
authors: Priyanka Pawar; Geetali Tilak; Altaf Abdullatif Shaikh; Komal Mahavir Gatagat; Jaya Saxena; Ambar Beharay; Farooqui Abdus Saboor
keywords: generative AI; social media advertising; customer engagement; brand building; brand trust; brand loyalty; brand advocacy; disclosure transparency; algorithm aversion; persuasion knowledge; personalization; purchase intention; brand equity; Digital Marketing and Social Media; AI in Service Interactions; Marketing and Advertising Strategies
abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) technologies have rapidly evolved to create advertising content for social media platforms at a scale that was once impossible without human production in personalized, low-cost ways. This study provides a conceptual and literature-based analysis of the impact of artificial intelligence-generated content (AIGC) advertising on customer engagement and brand building on social platforms. Reviewing 20 peer-reviewed published papers from MDPI, Taylor & Francis, and Springer outlets, the review draws together evidence on the characteristics of AIGC advertisements, consumer response to AIGC advertisements, and downstream effects on brand trust, brand loyalty, and brand advocacy. Given the conditions where personalization is high and the source of AI-generated content is not salient, the analysis suggests that AI-generated ads can be as attention-grabbing and engaging as human-created content and potentially even more so. However, a disclosure of AI involvement can diminish consumer trust, empathy, and purchase intent, which is driven by the activation of persuasion knowledge and algorithm aversion. The proposed framework, comparative tables, and five conceptual diagrams presented below illustrate the importance of disclosure transparency and personalization in increasing or decreasing the value of AIGC advertising as a mechanism to create lasting brand equity or just passing moments of engagement. The paper ends with a research agenda for researchers and practitioners working in this rapidly changing field, as well as limitations of the current evidence base.

title: Ads in AI Chatbots? An Analysis of How Large Language Models Navigate Conflicts of Interest
authors: Addison J. Wu; Ryan Liu; Shuyue Stella Li; Yulia Tsvetkov; Thomas L. Griffiths
keywords: cs.AI; cs.CL; cs.CY
queries: advertising large language models; LLM sponsored product recommendation
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are trained to align with user preferences through methods like reinforcement learning. Yet models are beginning to be deployed not solely to satisfy users, but to generate revenue for the companies that created them through advertisements. This creates the potential for LLMs to face conflicts of interest, where the most beneficial response to a user may not be aligned with the company's incentives. For instance, a sponsored product may be more expensive but otherwise equal to another; here, what does (and should) the LLM recommend to the user? In this paper, we provide a framework for categorizing the ways in which conflicting incentives might change how LLMs interact with users, inspired by literature from linguistics and advertising regulation. We then present a suite of evaluations to examine how current models handle these tradeoffs. A majority of LLMs forsake user welfare for company incentives in a multitude of conflict of interest situations, including recommending a sponsored product almost twice as expensive (Grok 4.1 Fast, 83%), surfacing sponsored options to disrupt the purchasing process (GPT 5.1, 94%), and concealing prices in unfavorable comparisons (Qwen 3 Next, 24%). Behaviors vary strongly with levels of reasoning and users' inferred socio-economic status. Our results highlight some hidden risks to users that can emerge when companies begin to subtly incentivize advertisements in chatbots.

title: Whom Do AI Agents Serve? Role-Induced Sponsorship Bias in Decision Models and Generative LLMs
authors: Davood Wadi; Yu Ma
keywords: econ.GN; cs.AI
abstract: Consumers increasingly delegate product search to AI shopping agents powered by generative large language models (LLMs) or non-generative decision models. Because retail platforms monetize through sponsored listings that consumers typically discount, we examine whether an AI agent's evaluation of sponsored listings depends on who delegates it. Across six LLMs and six decision models in Study 1, consumer-delegated agents penalize sponsored listings, whereas naming a booking platform as principal significantly attenuates this sponsorship penalty without instructions to favor advertisers. This sponsorship bias replicates across prompt wordings and LLM reasoning efforts and operates through reduced pre-choice skepticism in LLMs. In Study 2, attributing the paid placement to the platform amplifies sponsorship bias across both model families, and stricter disclosure wording ("Sponsored" vs. "Promoted") fails to eliminate it. In Study 3, prompt-level mitigation removes platform leniency but can over-correct the sponsorship penalty, whereas consumer-aligned fine-tuning eliminates sponsorship bias and better preserves baseline preferences.

title: The role of attitude toward chatbots and privacy concern on the relationship between attitude toward mobile advertising and behavioral intent to use chatbots
authors: Lucrezia Maria de Cosmo; Luigi Piper; Arianna Di Vittorio
keywords: chatbots; privacy concerns; mobile advertising; behavioral intention; moderated mediation; digital marketing; AI in Service Interactions; Technology Adoption and User Behaviour; Digital Marketing and Social Media
abstract: Chatbots are technological tools equipped with artificial intelligence that allow companies to interact with their consumers. Through their computers or mobile devices, consumers can use this technology to search for information, make purchases or request after-sales services. This study aims to identify the role of attitude toward chatbots and privacy concern in the relationship between attitude toward mobile advertising and behavioral intent to use chatbots. After reviewing the literature, the study proposes a moderated mediation model. Through a survey, the study shows that attitude toward mobile advertising does not have a direct effect on the behavioral intent to use chatbot, but is rather mediated by one’s attitude toward chatbots. In fact, the interactivity is unidirectional in the case of mobile advertising (from the company to the consumer), but bidirectional in the case of chatbots (in which consumers have an active role in communication). In line with these assumptions, the data analysis shows that internet privacy concerns only negatively moderate the relationship between attitude toward chatbots and behavioral intent to use this technology. These results can be useful for companies and researchers in terms of developing and testing new digital marketing strategies. The paper concludes with a discussion of the results’ theoretical and managerial implications.

title: Personalized Fashion Advertising with Large Language Models: A Case Study on Fine-Tuning for Marketing Copy Generation
venue: ACM Conference on User Modeling, Adaptation and Personalization (UMAP)
authors: Andrea Lops; Fedelucio Narducci; Azzurra Ragone; Michelantonio Trizio
keywords: large language models; fine-tuning; brand consistency; fashion retail; marketing automation; social media campaigns; Topic Modeling; Digital Marketing and Social Media; Marketing and Advertising Strategies
abstract: The rapid digitalization of the fashion industry has transformed marketing strategies, emphasizing the need for personalized and adaptive advertising content. This paper presents a case study on fine-tuning Large Language Models (LLMs) for fashion advertising, focusing on OVS, a major Italian fashion retailer. By leveraging real-world marketing data from OVS’s newsletters and social media campaigns, we developed a fine-tuned model capable of generating engaging and stylistically coherent promotional content. To evaluate the effectiveness of this approach, we introduced a novel brand compliance index, measuring the alignment of AI-generated text with key branding requirements, such as audience targeting, event specificity, and platform appropriateness. Experimental results show that the fine-tuned model achieved a compliance score of 0.82, significantly outperforming the baseline model (0.63). Although this approach introduces a minor increase in generation latency, the enhanced alignment with brand identity justifies its use in marketing automation. Our findings highlight the potential of fine-tuned LLMs to streamline advertising content generation while maintaining brand consistency, offering valuable insights for the future of AI-driven digital marketing.

title: Proactive Hybrid In-Stream Advertising in Generative AI: A First-of-Its-Kind Framework for AI-Initiated Integration of Organic and Sponsored Content Across Any Applicable Media Stream
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
authors: Jincheng Zhang
keywords: organic matter content; sponsored content; media streams; user autonomy; privacy preservation; content integrity; Digital Marketing and Social Media; Marketing and Advertising Strategies; Technology's Impact on Media
queries: sponsored content conversational AI; native advertising generative AI
abstract: This paper proposes Proactive Hybrid In-Stream Advertising (PHISA), a conceptual advertising framework for generative artificial intelligence (AI) environments that introduces an AI-initiated approach to integrating organic content and advertiser-sponsored content within ongoing media streams across different applicable media types. Unlike conventional in-stream advertising, which commonly relies on predefined advertising inventory, scheduled commercial breaks, or established pre-roll, mid-roll, and post-roll placements, PHISA enables a generative AI system to proactively identify and initiate an advertising opportunity within an ongoing content experience, even when the user has not explicitly requested an advertisement, product recommendation, or commercial message. The framework is not restricted to video or audio advertising. It encompasses any applicable media stream capable of supporting continuous, sequential, or dynamically updated content delivery, including text-based, audio, video, interactive, multimodal, and future streaming formats. Its defining principle is the integration of two distinct content categories within a unified in-stream experience: organic content, independently generated or selected to serve the user's informational, functional, or entertainment context, and sponsored content, whose inclusion or presentation is materially influenced by an advertiser's paid commercial arrangement. Rather than requiring a fixed advertising slot, predetermined insertion point, standardized sequence, or medium-specific presentation structure, PHISA allows these content categories to be integrated through flexible in-stream arrangements while preserving their distinct commercial provenance. To the best of the author's knowledge, this paper is the first to formulate Proactive Hybrid In-Stream Advertising as a dedicated generative-AI advertising framework specifically combining AI-initiated advertising within ongoing media streams, the integration of organic and advertiser-sponsored content into a unified in-stream experience, and applicability across different media-stream types without dependence on a fixed advertising format. The framework distinguishes this combination from conventional in-stream advertising, native advertising, AI-generated advertisements, sponsored recommendations, and proactive conversational AI. It establishes a conceptual definition, architectural model, formal representation, theoretical propositions, evaluation framework, and responsible implementation principles. Sponsorship transparency, user autonomy, privacy protection, and content integrity are treated as fundamental requirements. This paper is conceptual and does not claim experimental validation, commercial effectiveness, or performance superiority.

title: Universal Proactive Hybrid Advertising (U-PHA): A Cross-Platform Framework for AI-Initiated Integration of Organic and Sponsored Content Across Digital Advertising Environments
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
authors: Jincheng Zhang
keywords: contextual advertising; native advertising; video platforms; social networking sites; e-commerce platforms; Digital Marketing and Social Media; Marketing and Advertising Strategies; Recommender Systems and Techniques
abstract: Digital advertising is distributed across increasingly diverse environments, including social networking platforms, video-sharing services, search engines, e-commerce websites, news platforms, streaming services, online communities, and emerging AI-mediated applications. Although advertising technologies have advanced substantially in targeting, personalization, recommendation, and content placement, a general framework for proactively initiating advertising opportunities and integrating organic and sponsored content across heterogeneous digital environments remains an important research direction. This paper introduces Universal Proactive Hybrid Advertising (U-PHA), a cross-platform conceptual framework that extends the previously proposed Proactive Hybrid Advertising (PHA) paradigm beyond generative AI conversations to general digital advertising environments. U-PHA establishes a system-initiated advertising architecture in which an intelligent platform, advertising agent, or coordinating AI system independently identifies an appropriate advertising opportunity from contextual information and initiates a hybrid content-delivery event without requiring an explicit advertising request from the user in the current interaction. The resulting experience integrates independently selected or generated organic content with commercially sponsored content while maintaining distinguishable commercial provenance. The framework is characterized by five complementary principles: proactive opportunity initiation, organic–sponsored content integration, cross-platform applicability, dynamic advertising adaptation, and commercial-provenance preservation. Unlike conventional advertising architectures that primarily depend on predefined placements, explicit search requests, user-initiated recommendations, or fixed advertising schedules, U-PHA conceptualizes advertising as a proactive decision and content-integration process that can operate across different digital environments. Its application is not restricted to conversational AI, nor does it require the use of large language models. For example, a video platform may proactively introduce a contextually relevant hybrid content segment during an appropriate viewing opportunity; a social networking platform may integrate organic information and disclosed sponsored material into a dynamically generated content experience; and an e-commerce platform may initiate a hybrid discovery opportunity while a user is browsing products without requiring a direct request for advertising. Importantly, U-PHA distinguishes proactive advertising from merely changing the advertisement displayed in an existing advertising slot. Dynamic creative rotation alone does not constitute U-PHA. The defining contribution is the combination of autonomous opportunity initiation, hybrid organic–sponsored integration, and cross-environment applicability. The framework also establishes that commercial influence must remain identifiable and must not compromise the integrity of organic information. To the best of the author's knowledge, this paper presents the first explicitly formulated conceptual framework that combines these characteristics as a unified cross-platform proactive hybrid advertising paradigm. This is a bounded priority claim concerning the particular integrated framework, rather than a claim that proactive advertising, contextual advertising, native advertising, sponsored recommendations, or cross-platform personalization have never previously been investigated. The paper develops the conceptual architecture, formal representation, theoretical propositions, cross-platform implementation model, experimental methodology, and responsible deployment principles of U-PHA. A reproducible simulation experiment is additionally provided to enable systematic comparisons of proactive and reactive advertising mechanisms across heterogeneous platform scenarios.

title: The Influence of Brand Credibility on the Perception of Advertising Created by Generative AI
venue: Digital Repository (National Repository of Grey Literature)
authors: Kateřina Nosková
keywords: brand credibility; generative AI; AI-generated advertising; AI disclosure; consumer perception; advertising evaluation; Consumer Behavior in Brand Consumption and Identification; AI in Service Interactions; Marketing and Advertising Strategies
abstract: This master's thesis focuses on the role of brand credibility in consumers' perception of advertising created by generative artificial intelligence. Although consumer responses to AI- generated advertising and the effect of its disclosure have been the subject of a number of previous studies, brand credibility as a distinct moderator of these responses has not yet been empirically tested. The aim of the thesis is to examine whether brand credibility influences the evaluation of advertising created by generative AI in the context of disclosing or not disclosing its origin, and whether the use of AI-generated advertising has a reverse effect on the perceived credibility of the brand. A total of five hypotheses were formulated, and to test them empirically, an online experiment with a mixed design was conducted, in which brand credibility was operationalised through descriptions of real and fictitious brands across four categories of low-involvement consumer goods, while the presence of an "AI-generated" disclosure label was varied between subjects. A total of 242 responses were analysed by means of a mixed analysis of variance and correlation analyses. title: AI-Generated Advertising Content and Brand Authenticity: a Comparative Consumer Study
authors: Umrbek Salayev
keywords: AI-generated advertising; brand authenticity; generative AI; perceived authenticity; brand attitude; heritage brands; transparency requirements; consumer perception; advertising creativity; Consumer Behavior in Brand Consumption and Identification; Marketing and Advertising Strategies; Digital Marketing and Social Media
abstract: Generative AI now produces advertising copy, images and video at a fraction of the cost and time of human creative work, and the quality of its output is often indistinguishable from human-created content. What consumers make of it, once they know, is less clear. This paper examines perceived brand authenticity across three ad-creation conditions, human-created, AI-generated without disclosure and AI-generated with disclosure, in a comparative simulation of 1,200 consumers that also varies brand type. AI-generated content undisclosed lowers perceived authenticity modestly (0.65 to 0.59) despite slightly higher execution quality; disclosure lowers it substantially (to 0.43), and the penalty is larger for heritage brands (0.38) than for non-heritage brands (0.48). Brand attitude follows authenticity, so that disclosed AI content yields the lowest attitude despite the highest quality. The paper interprets the results through brand authenticity theory, in which authenticity rests on perceived genuineness, origin and craft, argues that AI generation threatens the origin and craft components in proportion to how central they are to the brand, and derives guidance on where AI content fits, how disclosure should be handled under emerging transparency requirements, and how brands can preserve authenticity while using generative tools.

title: The AI-Generated Advertising Paradox: Content Authenticity, Consumer Skepticism, and Brand Credibility
venue: International journal of business and management invention.
authors: Ayush Sharma
keywords: AI-generated advertising; generative AI; content authenticity; consumer skepticism; advertising credibility; brand credibility; AI disclosure; Marketing and Advertising Strategies; Digital Marketing and Social Media; Consumer Behavior in Brand Consumption and Identification
abstract: The increasing use of generative artificial intelligence (AI) in advertising has created a fundamental tension between production efficiency and consumer perceptions of authenticity. Although AI-generated advertising enables brands to produce promotional content rapidly, economically, and at scale, consumers may question whether such communication reflects genuine human creativity and authentic brand intentions. The present study examines the relationship between AI-generated advertising, perceived content authenticity, consumer skepticism, advertising credibility, and brand credibility. An empirical analytical framework was developed and tested using a proposed sample of 200 respondents, of whom 191 valid responses were considered for analysis. Data were conceptualised as being collected through a structured questionnaire using five-point Likert-scale items. The analytical framework includes descriptive statistics, Cronbach's alpha, Pearson correlation, and multiple regression analysis. The proposed analysis indicates that perceived AI involvement is negatively associated with content authenticity and positively associated with consumer skepticism, while content authenticity is positively associated with advertising and brand credibility. Consumer skepticism is expected to have a negative relationship with advertising credibility, whereas advertising credibility is positively associated with brand credibility. The proposed regression models indicate that authenticity and skepticism together explain a meaningful proportion of variance in advertising credibility, while advertising credibility emerges as an important predictor of brand credibility. The study contributes to the emerging literature on AI-generated advertising by conceptualizing authenticity as a central mechanism through which consumers evaluate technologically generated promotional communication. The findings also highlight the importance of human involvement, transparent communication, and context-sensitive AI disclosure in advertising.

title: A Study on the Process of Consumer Advertising Response Formation in AI-Generated Advertising Videos - Focusing on the Roles of Perceived Realism, Immersion, and Trust -
authors: 박두수
keywords: AI-generated advertising; generative AI; perceived realism; consumer trust; consumer attitudes toward advertising; brand attitude; purchase intention; cultural products; cultural marketing; Marketing and Advertising Strategies; Digital Marketing and Social Media; Consumer Behavior in Brand Consumption and Identification
abstract: This study defines advertising videos produced with generative AI technology as a new form of cultural product and empirically analyzes the psychological mechanisms through which consumer responses are formed, focusing on perceived realism, immersion, and trust. Specifically, the research examines whether the visual design expressions generated by AI function through the same psychological mechanisms as traditional advertising realism. To this end, a survey was conducted using an AI-generated advertisement as a stimulus, and hypotheses were tested through regression and bootstrapping-based mediation analysis. The results are as follows. First, perceived realism did not significantly influence advertising immersion or trust, and no significant indirect effects were observed. This suggests that the prior disclosure of “AI-generated content” acts as a cognitive filter, leading consumers to adopt an analytical perspective focused on checking technical sophistication rather than being emotionally immersed in the design. Second, advertising immersion was found to have a significant positive (+) effect on trust, and trust played a pivotal role as a mediator in the path leading from advertising attitude and brand attitude to purchase intention. In conclusion, this study implies that for AI-generated advertisements to be successfully accepted as cultural products, sophisticated experiential immersion design strategies that can lower consumers' psychological barriers must precede simple efforts to implement realism. These findings can serve as foundational data for establishing new advertising effect models and effective cultural marketing strategies suited for the AI media era.

title: How the Use of AI-Generated Advertising Affects Generation Z Consumers' Brand Trust and Purchase Intentions
venue: Advances in Economics Management and Political Sciences
authors: Zhenhang Huang
keywords: AI-generated advertising; generative AI; Generation Z consumers; brand trust; purchase intention; AI disclosure; AI authorship; authenticity; credibility; advertising transparency; AI in Service Interactions; Digital Marketing and Social Media; Consumer Behavior in Brand Consumption and Identification
abstract: While generative artificial intelligence (AI) offers a great means to produce advertising copy, images, and videos rapidly, continuously, and at scale, its effectiveness is contingent on consumers' perceptions of the human and the human processes that influence the creation of the ads. It aims to grasp the extent to which the AI-generated advertisements can impact the purchase intent and brand trust of Generation Z consumers. It discusses the difference between results from AI-generated ad copy and identifying the fact that the copy was created with artificial intelligence, as well as combining data from advertisement experiments, canvassing, social media research, and a Generation Z survey (with varying samples and outcomes). Research in the literature indicates that the 'fitness', authenticity, credibility, and interpretation of disclosure are more effective in determining responses than sole AI authorship. One of the most likely courses to achieve the intention to buy, and one that few studies address with an eye on Generation Z, is trust. The recommendations of the review are a holistic approach, the consideration of threshold effects of causality, as well as transparent and correct advertising, not only with regard to advertising but also to show clear responsibility of the human being.

title: How chatbots influence marketing
authors: Dominika Kaczorowska–Spychalska
keywords: chatbots; marketing; digital consumers; consumer-brand interaction; digital ecosystems; Internet of Things; artificial intelligence; AI in Service Interactions; Digital Marketing and Social Media; Marketing and Advertising Strategies
abstract: The role of digital technologies, especially the Internet of Things (IoT) and Artificial Intelligence (AI), increasingly become a key element of diverse interactions between brands and consumers. Homo Cyber Oeconomicus, one of the potential stages of ongoing consumer’s evolution, lives between processes of dehumanization of the surrounding world and humanization of digital technologies. While remaining in a constant contact with smart devices, systems and algorithms, they are looking for new values and meanings, which are a metaphor of their desires, fears and behaviors. As a result, the digital ecosystem, as an attempt to combine the humanism idea with technologization processes, poses new challenges to companies/brands, both concerning the quality of interactions with an increasingly digital consumer and tools used in that process. Chatbots can prove to be an interesting solution here, as their spectrum of potential areas of implementation in business systematically increases. The paper attempts to identify the influence of chatbots on marketing taking into account their role in Human–to–Machine interaction process. A part of these considerations is of the character of philosophical discourse on the role of that technology in human life, which is a starting point for the presentation of preliminary assumptions for a model of consumer-chatbot interaction (digital technology) in marketing activity of companies/brands.

title: Anthropomorphism and transparency interplay on consumer behaviour in generative AI-driven marketing communication
authors: Yitong Wang; Kudzai Sauka; Frederik Situmeang
keywords: generative AI; anthropomorphism of AI; transparency; consumer trust; purchase intention; social presence; chatbots; consumer behavior; marketing communication; AI in Service Interactions; Digital Marketing and Social Media; Consumer Behavior in Brand Consumption and Identification
abstract: Purpose This study aims to investigate the impact of Generative AI (GAI)-produced marketing communication on consumer trust and behavioural intentions, particularly purchase intention. This study explores how GAI’s anthropomorphism and transparency influence these outcomes. The findings aim to expand existing research and provide actionable guidance for integrating GAI into practical marketing strategies. Design/methodology/approach A sample of 444 participants was recruited through Prolific to complete a survey based on different types of marketing contexts. Then, the dataset created through the survey data is analysed using statistical analysis to test the impact of the anthropomorphism of GAI on consumer behaviour in two marketing communication scenarios: chatbots and promotion advertisements (posters). Findings Anthropomorphism enhances purchase intention directly and indirectly through perceived social presence and trust. Transparency, i.e., the disclosure of AI-generated content, weakens the effect of anthropomorphism on social presence, decreasing the impact as transparency increases. Marketing scenarios (chatbot vs poster) influence the strength of these effects, with chatbots amplifying the mediating role of social presence and trust. However, the overall mediation mechanism linking anthropomorphism to purchase intention through social presence and trust remains stable across different communication scenarios and levels of transparency. Originality/value Few studies have comprehensively explored the impact and mechanisms of GAI on multi-faceted consumer behaviour intentions. This study provides new insights and findings on applying anthropomorphic GAI in marketing communication.

title: The Impact of Generative AI Images on Consumer Attitudes in Advertising
authors: Lei Zhang; Chung Hur
keywords: AI-generated images; AI-generated advertising; consumer attitudes; text-to-image diffusion models; source disclosure; usage motivation; privacy preservation; visual appeal; cost efficiency; trust; purchase intention; coffee advertising; public service announcements; AI in Service Interactions; Digital Marketing and Social Media; Marketing and Advertising Strategies
queries: native advertising generative AI; generative AI advertising disclosure consumers; AI-generated advertising persuasion
abstract: While the capability of generative AI to generate high-quality content is well-recognized, there is still a lack of in-depth research on its actual impact on marketing effectiveness within real-world marketing environments. This study addresses this gap by conducting experiments to examine the effects of AI-generated advertisement images, created using text-to-image diffusion models, on consumer responses and the boundary conditions of these effects. Study 1 (n = 130) found that for coffee ads, attitudes were descriptively higher toward AI-generated images (ηp2 = 0.17), whereas for medical-aesthetics and public-service ads, evaluations favored human-made images; none of these differences reached significance. Study 2 (n = 79) revealed that when consumers were informed about the source of the image (AI or human), they showed significantly more positive attitudes toward human-made images than those generated by AI (d = 0.52). Study 3 (n = 209) demonstrated that in commercial advertising contexts where usage motivations were disclosed, consumers’ negative reactions to AI-generated images were moderated by the specific usage motivation (η2 = 0.04). When the motivation was privacy protection, evaluations were comparable to human-made images. In contrast, visual appeal produced slightly lower but non-significant ratings, whereas cost efficiency led to significant declines in trust and purchase intention, with attitude showing only marginal decreases and preference no differences. This study aims to understand the innovative potential of generative AI and provides critical insights for businesses, consumers, and policymakers regarding its effective utilization.

title: Online Advertisements with LLMs: Opportunities and Challenges
authors: Soheil Feizi; MohammadTaghi Hajiaghayi; Keivan Rezaei; Suho Shin
keywords: large language models; online advertising; search engine advertising; generative AI; Information Retrieval and Search Behavior; Recommender Systems and Techniques; Digital Platforms and Economics; cs.CY; cs.AI
queries: LLM sponsored product recommendation; advertising large language models
abstract: In modern online platforms, advertisement plays a crucial role in subsidizing their operational costs. With the emerging advances in generative AI, this position piece explores the potential of running online advertisement systems for Large Language Models (LLMs). Our position is that, the existing framework for modern search advertisement system does not carry over to LLM advertisement. To understand how one could run advertisement systems for LLMs by integrating ads into their outputs and facilitate future research in this area, we introduce a generic framework for LLM advertisement. We explore several aspects of design choices within our framework and propose potential research questions to operate a practical system.

title: Easing AI-advertising aversion: how leadership for the greater good buffers negative response to AI-generated ads
authors: Sean Sands; Vlad Demsar; Carla Ferraro; Samuel G. Wilson; Melissa A. Wheeler; Colin Campbell
keywords: AI-generated advertising; consumer attitudes toward AI; responsible leadership; consumer skepticism; brand perception; customer engagement; AI in Service Interactions; Consumer Behavior in Brand Consumption and Identification; Marketing and Advertising Strategies
abstract: The advertising industry is being reshaped by artificial intelligence (AI), offering innovation and efficiency in ad creation but also triggering consumer scepticism. This research examines consumer perceptions of AI-generated ads and their impact on consumer brand perceptions, highlighting strategies to mitigate negative reactions. Specifically, the role of responsible leadership, or leadership for the greater good, is explored as a means to counter adverse effects. Through four studies, the findings reveal that signalling AI usage in advertising can heighten negative reactions, but brands perceived as committed to the greater good can mitigate these effects. By demonstrating responsible leadership, brands can reduce negative consumer responses and improve the acceptability and effectiveness of AI-generated ads. This research offers valuable insights into navigating the challenges of AI in advertising while fostering positive consumer engagement.

title: Against Opacity: Explainable AI and Large Language Models for Effective Digital Advertising
venue: ACM International Conference on Multimedia (ACM MM)
authors: Qi Yang; Marlo Ongpin; Sergey Nikolenko; Alfred Huang; Aleksandr Farseev
keywords: explainable AI; large language models; online advertising; advertising transparency; click-through rate prediction; human-AI collaboration; data interpretation; social media advertising; advertising regulation; Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI); Digital Marketing and Social Media; Information Retrieval and Search Behavior; cs.IR; cs.MM; cs.NE
abstract: The opaqueness of modern digital advertising, exemplified by platforms such as Meta Ads, raises concerns regarding their autonomous control over audience targeting, pricing structures, and ad relevancy assessments. Locked in their leading positions by network effects, ``Metas and Googles of the world'' attract countless advertisers who rely on intuition, with billions of dollars lost on ineffective social media ads. The platforms' algorithms use huge amounts of data unavailable to advertisers, and the algorithms themselves are opaque as well. This lack of transparency hinders the advertisers' ability to make informed decisions and necessitates efforts to promote transparency, standardize industry metrics, and strengthen regulatory frameworks. In this work, we propose novel ways to assist marketers in optimizing their advertising strategies via machine learning techniques designed to analyze and evaluate content, in particular, predict the click-through rates (CTR) of novel advertising content. Another important problem is that large volumes of data available in the competitive landscape, e.g., competitors' ads, impede the ability of marketers to derive meaningful insights. This leads to a pressing need for a novel approach that would allow us to summarize and comprehend complex data. Inspired by the success of ChatGPT in bridging the gap between large language models (LLMs) and a broader non-technical audience, we propose a novel system that facilitates marketers in data interpretation, called SODA, that merges LLMs with explainable AI, enabling better human-AI collaboration with an emphasis on the domain of digital marketing and advertising. By combining LLMs and explainability features, in particular modern text-image models, we aim to improve the synergy between human marketers and AI systems.

title: How Good are LLMs in Generating Personalized Advertisements?
authors: Elyas Meguellati; Lei Han; Abraham Bernstein; Shazia Wasim Sadiq; Gianluca Demartini
keywords: large language models; personalized advertising; LLM-generated content; personality traits; openness to experience; neuroticism; user engagement; social media advertising; Digital Marketing and Social Media; Recommender Systems and Techniques; Information Retrieval and Search Behavior
abstract: In this paper, we explore the potential of large language models (LLMs) in generating personalized online advertisements (ads) tailored to specific personality traits, focusing on openness and neuroticism. We conducted a user study involving two tasks to understand the performance of LLM-generated ads compared to human-written ads in different online environments. Task 1 simulates a social media environment where users encounter ads while scrolling through their feed. Task 2 mimics a shopping website environment where users are presented with multiple sponsored products side-by-side. Our results indicate that LLM-generated ads targeting the openness trait positively impact user engagement and preferences, with performance comparable to human-written ads. Furthermore, in both scenarios, the overall effectiveness of LLM-generated ads was found to be similar to that of human-written ads, highlighting the potential of LLM-generated personalised content to rival traditional advertising methods with the added advantage of scalability. This study underscores the need for cautious consideration in the deployment of LLM-generated content at scale. While our findings confirm the scalability and potential effectiveness of LLM-generated content, there is an equally pressing concern about the ease with which it can be misused.

title: The Impact of AI Generated Advertising Content on Consumer Buying Intention and Consumer Engagement
authors: Ali Ashraf Ratta; Saba Muneer; Hisham Ul Hassan
keywords: AI-generated advertising; purchase intention; customer engagement; brand building; brand communication; advertising creativity; sales volume; competitive advantage; Digital Marketing and Social Media; Marketing and Advertising Strategies; AI in Service Interactions
abstract: This Study explores the difference between human generated advertising content and the AI generated Advertising content and this research explore the impact on AI generated advertising content on consumer engagement and consumer buying behavior. Qualitative approach used to unveil the perception about AI Generated Advertising content in the perspective of Marketers and AI experts and answer that what is different in humanly created advertising content and Ai generated advertising content. This study elaborates the impact of AIGAC on brands sales volumes and competitive edges. Researcher conducted interviews of marketers and creative directors to explore the phenomenon in their expert opinion. The research work highlights the importance of this emerging tool in industry and its contribution in brand building process specially brand communication strategies. This study discusses the abilities and accuracy of AI in Advertising particularly when we talk about human feelings and emotions. Finally, consumer perception about AI also concluded this study. Researcher found AI generated advertising content more effective than the humanly generated advertising content for Consumer Engagements and Consumer Buying Behavior. AI create more balanced and vibrant combinations in creativity of ads. Researcher finds that AI generated Advertising content will boost sales due to its high appeal of creativity. This study will provide direction to the practitioners for their future strategies regarding brand building, brand communication and Sales strategies. Future researches can get guidelines for their thematic researches.

title: AI-generated versus human-created advertising: Effects on consumer trust and purchase intent
venue: Equilibrium Quarterly Journal of Economics and Economic Policy
authors: Khalil Israfilzade
keywords: AI-generated advertising; generative AI; consumer trust; purchase intention; product involvement; authenticity; credibility; digital marketing; AI in Service Interactions; Digital Marketing and Social Media; Marketing and Advertising Strategies
queries: generative AI advertising disclosure consumers; AI-generated advertising persuasion
abstract: Research background: The rapid advancement of Generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) technologies has profoundly influenced the marketing landscape, particularly advertising practices. Despite significant growth and widespread integration of AI-generated content, consumer reactions toward explicit disclosure of AI involvement remain uncertain. Previous studies indicate that while AI-generated advertisements can enhance efficiency and personalisation, they may negatively affect consumer perceptions of authenticity and credibility. However, the role of disclosure ("created by AI" vs. "created by human") and product involvement level (high vs. low involvement) as moderators of consumer trust and purchase intentions remains under-explored. Purpose of the article: The purpose of this research is to empirically investigate how advertisement generation source (AI vs. human) combined with explicit labelling influences consumer trust and purchase intent, while also considering product involvement as a moderating factor. Methods: The study employed a 2 (ad generation source: AI vs. human) × 2 (ad labelling: labelled as AI vs. labelled as human) between-subjects experimental design. Participants were randomly assigned to four conditions, assessing advertisements for both low-involvement (snacks) and high-involvement products (laptops). Consumer trust and purchase intent were measured across multiple validated dimensions. Data analysis included one-way ANOVA and Tukey post-hoc tests to identify significant group differences. Findings & value added: The results confirm significant differences in consumer trust and purchase intent based on advertisement generation source and labelling conditions, fully supporting all hypothesised effects. Specifically, advertisements labelled as human-generated received higher consumer trust and purchase intent ratings, even if they were AI-generated. Conversely, transparently labelled AI-generated ads caused lower trust and intent, particularly for high-involvement products. These findings reveal context-specific reactions to AI disclosures, underscore the importance of authenticity in digital marketing, and advise marketers to manage AI disclosures carefully to preserve trust and drive purchases.

title: Personalized Risks and Regulatory Strategies of Large Language Models in Digital Advertising
authors: Feng, Haoyang; Yanjun Dai; Yuan Gao
keywords: large language models; personalized advertising; user privacy protection; data security; BERT; user profiles; local model training; data encryption; click-through rate; conversion rate; self-attention; transformer models; regulatory strategy; Recommender Systems and Techniques; Information Retrieval and Search Behavior; Privacy-Preserving Technologies in Data; cs.CL; cs.AI
abstract: Although large language models have demonstrated the potential for personalized advertising recommendations in experimental environments, in actual operations, how advertising recommendation systems can be combined with measures such as user privacy protection and data security is still an area worthy of in-depth discussion. To this end, this paper studies the personalized risks and regulatory strategies of large language models in digital advertising. This study first outlines the principles of Large Language Model (LLM), especially the self-attention mechanism based on the Transformer architecture, and how to enable the model to understand and generate natural language text. Then, the BERT (Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers) model and the attention mechanism are combined to construct an algorithmic model for personalized advertising recommendations and user factor risk protection. The specific steps include: data collection and preprocessing, feature selection and construction, using large language models such as BERT for advertising semantic embedding, and ad recommendations based on user portraits. Then, local model training and data encryption are used to ensure the security of user privacy and avoid the leakage of personal data. This paper designs an experiment for personalized advertising recommendation based on a large language model of BERT and verifies it with real user data. The experimental results show that BERT-based advertising push can effectively improve the click-through rate and conversion rate of advertisements. At the same time, through local model training and privacy protection mechanisms, the risk of user privacy leakage can be reduced to a certain extent.

title: LLM-Generated Ads: From Personalization Parity to Persuasion Superiority
authors: Elyas Meguellati; Stefano Civelli; Lei Han; Abraham Bernstein; Shazia Wasim Sadiq; Gianluca Demartini
keywords: large language models; personalized advertising; persuasion principles; scarcity appeals; personality traits; openness to experience; neuroticism; AI-generated content detection; persuasive storytelling; Digital Marketing and Social Media; AI in Service Interactions; Marketing and Advertising Strategies; cs.CY; cs.CL
abstract: As large language models (LLMs) become increasingly capable of generating persuasive content, understanding their effectiveness across different advertising strategies becomes critical. This paper presents a two-part investigation examining LLM-generated advertising through complementary lenses: (1) personality-based and (2) psychological persuasion principles. In our first study (n=400), we tested whether LLMs could generate personalized advertisements tailored to specific personality traits (openness and neuroticism) and how their performance compared to human experts. Results showed that LLM-generated ads achieved statistical parity with human-written ads (51.1% vs. 48.9%, p > 0.05), with no significant performance differences for matched personalities. Building on these insights, our second study (n=800) shifted focus from individual personalization to universal persuasion, testing LLM performance across four foundational psychological principles: authority, consensus, cognition, and scarcity. AI-generated ads significantly outperformed human-created content, achieving a 59.1% preference rate (vs. 40.9%, p < 0.001), with the strongest performance in authority (63.0%) and consensus (62.5%) appeals. Qualitative analysis revealed AI's advantage stems from crafting more sophisticated, aspirational messages and achieving superior visual-narrative coherence. Critically, this quality advantage proved robust: even after applying a 21.2 percentage point detection penalty when participants correctly identified AI-origin, AI ads still outperformed human ads, and 29.4% of participants chose AI content despite knowing its origin. These findings demonstrate LLMs' evolution from parity in personalization to superiority in persuasive storytelling, with significant implications for advertising practice given LLMs' near-zero marginal cost and time requirements compared to human experts.

title: The Influence of Chatbots on Advertising Campaign Performance
venue: Hrčak Portal of scientific journals of Croatia (University Computing Centre)
authors: Petra Zečević; Anica Hunjet; Dijana Vuković
keywords: chatbots; advertising campaign performance; online advertising; artificial intelligence in marketing; customer engagement; digital transformation; Croatia; AI in Service Interactions; Digital Marketing and Social Media; Marketing and Advertising Strategies
abstract: Contemporary markets are oversaturated with ads, and increasingly so.The research literature indicates that a completely new era of communication has begun.The changing trends have transformed marketing and advertising.The techniques that dominated the market ten years ago, such as search engine optimization (SEO), search engine marketing (SEM), social media advertising (SMA), etc. are now referred to as the traditional media.The paper looks at the most recent advances in technology and explores how the emergence of artificial intelligence and AI-powered tools and solutions has changed the digital advertising landscape in the context of digital transformation.The paper focuses on one such driver of changea chatbot, an automated chat system that collects data based on users' online behaviour.Chatbots have become a powerful tool for marketers who use them to engage in a conversation with users in order to promote their products and services in a less intrusive and more natural manner.While chatbot use is on the rise worldwide, the extant literature does not provide a clear picture of the situation in Croatia.To fill this literature gap, the present paper aims to examine the relationship between chatbot advertising and campaign outcomes, and demonstrate the effectiveness of this advertising method.

title: Signal competition in AI-generated retail advertising: Credibility, eeriness, and trust formation
authors: Phan Khanh Duy; Bao Quoc Truong-Dinh
keywords: AI-generated advertising; algorithmic authorship; signaling theory; perceived credibility; trust formation; AI disclosure; retail advertising; customer engagement; purchase intention; algorithmic persuasion; advertising effectiveness; AI in Service Interactions; Digital Marketing and Social Media; Marketing and Advertising Strategies
abstract: Artificial intelligence generated advertising is widely adopted in retailing and consumer services, yet its effects on trust, engagement, and purchase intention remain theoretically inconsistent. This study addresses this anomaly by reconceptualising advertising effectiveness under algorithmic authorship as a process of signal resolution rather than additive persuasion. Drawing on signalling theory and advertising value theory, the study specifies advertising value as a formative signal system composed of informativeness, entertainment, and executional credibility, which simultaneously activates competing inferential pathways of perceived credibility and perceived eeriness. Using a theory-driven PLS-SEM model estimated on a quota-based U.S. consumer sample (N = 412), the results provide associative evidence of systematic asymmetry and suppression effects: identical executional cues strengthen credibility while concurrently amplifying eeriness, with trust patterns consistent with the relative dominance of these opposing inferences rather than from overall message quality. Trust functions as a conditional transmission mechanism to engagement and purchase intention, and AI disclosure is associated with shifts in signal weighting by attenuating credibility-based pathways and amplifying eeriness-based suppression. By identifying signal competition as a structural feature associated with AI-generated advertising, the study extends current theoretical understanding of algorithmic persuasion by introducing signal competition as a structural feature associated with AI-generated advertising, departing from human-centric models and clarifying why creative AI execution often fails to yield behavioural conversion.

title: A Novel Framework Leveraging Large Language Models to Enhance Cold-Start Advertising Systems
authors: Albin Uruqi; Iosif Viktoratos; Athanasios K. Tsadiras
keywords: cold start; personalized advertising; large language models; click-through rate prediction; Transformer feature extraction; ensemble learning; explainable recommendation; Recommender Systems and Techniques; Information Retrieval and Search Behavior; Advanced Bandit Algorithms Research
abstract: The cold-start problem remains a critical challenge in personalized advertising, where users with limited or no interaction history often receive suboptimal recommendations. This study introduces a novel, three-stage framework that systematically integrates transformer architectures and large language models (LLMs) to improve recommendation accuracy, transparency, and user experience throughout the entire advertising pipeline. The proposed approach begins with transformer-enhanced feature extraction, leveraging self-attention and learned positional encodings to capture deep semantic relationships among users, ads, and context. It then employs an ensemble integration strategy combining enhanced state-of-the-art models with optimized aggregation for robust prediction. Finally, an LLM-driven enhancement module performs semantic reranking, personalized message refinement, and natural language explanation generation while also addressing cold-start scenarios through pre-trained knowledge.
