The LLM component further supports diversification, fairness-aware ranking, and sentiment sensitivity in order to ensure more relevant, diverse, and ethically grounded recommendations. Extensive experiments on DigiX and Avazu datasets demonstrate notable gains in click-through rate prediction (CTR), while an in-depth real user evaluation showcases improvements in perceived ad relevance, message quality, transparency, and trust. This work advances the state-of-the-art by combining CTR models with interpretability and contextual reasoning. The strengths of the proposed method, such as its innovative integration of components, empirical validation, multifaceted LLM application, and ethical alignment highlight its potential as a robust, future-ready solution for personalized advertising.

title: LLM Advertisement based on Neuron Auctions
authors: Peiran Yun; Wenxin Xu; Jiayuan Liu; Yihang Zhang; Liang Zeng; Lingkai Kong; Tonghan Wang
keywords: large language models; mechanistic interpretability; auction design; strategy-proofness; user utility; Auction Theory and Applications; Recommender Systems and Techniques; Topic Modeling
abstract: As Large Language Models (LLMs) transition into conversational agents, generative advertising emerges as a crucial monetization strategy. However, embedding advertisements within unstructured LLM outputs introduces a critical trilemma: balancing advertiser payoffs, platform revenue, and user experience. Existing methods, such as prompt injection or rigid position slots, disrupt semantic coherence and lack a parametric framework for independent control, rendering rigorous mechanism design intractable. To bridge this gap, we introduce Neuron Auctions, a novel paradigm that shifts the auction object from the surface text space to the LLM's internal representations. Leveraging mechanistic interpretability, we identify brand-specific feed-forward network (FFN) neurons and demonstrate that competing brands activate within approximately orthogonal subspaces. This near-perfect independence allows us to define continuous, disentangled intervention budgets (specifically, neuron counts and amplification factors) as auctionable commodities. Building on this computational carrier, we design a continuous menu-based auction mechanism that naturally guarantees strategy-proofness and optimizes revenue for the platform. By explicitly incorporating a user utility penalty into the platform's optimization objective, our framework dynamically prices out overly aggressive interventions. Extensive experiments demonstrate that Neuron Auctions effectively preserve natural discourse quality while achieving an optimal alignment between commercial incentives and user satisfaction.

title: Large language models in advertising: Unlocking potential and understanding boundaries
venue: World Journal of Advanced Engineering Technology and Sciences
authors: Arun Thomas
keywords: large language models; advertising; content creation; audience targeting; real-time bidding; brand voice; factual accuracy; hybrid systems; AI ethics; advertising compliance; LLM evaluation; Topic Modeling; Artificial Intelligence Applications; Information Retrieval and Search Behavior
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are revolutionizing the advertising industry by introducing unprecedented capabilities that transform creative processes, audience targeting, and campaign management. This technical review explores how these sophisticated neural network architectures integrate into advertising ecosystems while examining both their transformative potential and implementation challenges. LLMs demonstrate exceptional abilities in generating diverse advertising content, expanding semantic keyword understanding, modeling user intent with nuance, and automating campaign workflows. However, several obstacles hinder their seamless integration, including latency constraints incompatible with real-time bidding environments, inconsistent outputs that complicate brand voice maintenance, prompt instability requiring continuous refinement, and factual accuracy concerns that present compliance risks. The review proposes technical solutions such as multi-layered guardrail architectures, hybrid system designs that strategically deploy LLMs alongside deterministic systems, specialized evaluation frameworks beyond standard metrics, and ethical implementation guidelines. Future directions include advertising-focused model development, real-time optimization capabilities, multimodal applications spanning text and visual content, and comprehensive governance frameworks that balance innovation with responsible deployment considerations.

title: Generative AI Advertising as a Problem of Trustworthy Commercial Intervention
authors: Jingyi Qiu; Qiaozhu Mei
keywords: large language models; commercial influence; information framing; retrieval-augmented generation; agentic AI; user autonomy; Ethics and Social Impacts of AI; Digitalization, Law, and Regulation; Technology's Impact on Media; cs.CY; cs.CL
queries: native advertising generative AI; advertising large language models
abstract: Major deployed generative AI advertising systems preserve a visible boundary between commercial content and AI-generated responses. Yet empirical research shows that ads woven directly into large language model (LLM) outputs often go undetected by users. We argue that generative AI fundamentally changes advertising: rather than placing products into discrete slots, it enables interventions on the generative process itself, which induce commercial influence through less observable channels. This reframes generative AI advertising as a problem of trustworthy intervention rather than content placement. We introduce a taxonomy organized by influence tier, corresponding to interventions on progressively more latent variables: product mentions, information framing, behavioral redirection, and long-term preference shaping; and show how these tiers instantiate across modalities and system architectures, including retrieval-augmented generation and agentic pipelines where upstream decisions can sharply constrain downstream outcomes. Both major deployed systems and designed mechanisms concentrate on the most observable and easiest-to-govern tier, while the forms of commercial influence most consequential for user autonomy remain poorly understood and lack frameworks for detection, measurement, or disclosure. The central challenge is whether commercial influence in generative systems can be made trustworthy, i.e., attributable, measurable, contestable, and aligned with user welfare.

title: Evaluating Brand Retrieval and Ranking in Large Language Model Recommendations
authors: Edward Carl Malthouse; Kun-Yu Lee; Jing Yang; Sanchary Pal; Xueyan Feng
keywords: large language models; recommendation evaluation; brand recommendation; recommendation ranking; mean reciprocal rank; brand popularity; search interest; product recommendation; Information Retrieval and Search Behavior; Recommender Systems and Techniques; Topic Modeling
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for product recommendation, but evaluating their recommendations presents challenges that differ from conventional information retrieval and recommender systems. LLMs can generate recommendations without an explicit candidate set, and repeated responses to the same query can produce different brands and rankings. We introduce a framework for evaluating open-ended LLM brand recommendations that defines the competitive set independently of model outputs and estimates recommendation prevalence and prominence through repeated sampling. We operationalize these constructs using Brand Recommendation Probability (BRP@$k$) and Mean Reciprocal Rank (MRR@$k$), and apply the framework to six LLMs across five product categories. Category-only queries reveal substantial omission of established brands and limited evidence that recommendation prominence follows conventional brand popularity. Instead, prominence is associated with broader marketplace-visibility signals, particularly search interest and online brand conversation. Needs-based queries show that contextualizing users' goals and constraints changes which brands are retrieved, while diagnostic positioning probes demonstrate that brands omitted from ordinary recommendations can remain conditionally retrievable when distinctive cues are supplied. These findings highlight the need to evaluate LLM recommendation as a stochastic retrieval-and-ranking process rather than from individual generated lists. We provide open-source software and data to support reproducible evaluation of LLM-generated brand recommendations.

title: Consumer Attitude Towards AI-Generated Advertisement
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
authors: Shaily Raj; Sabeeha Fatima
keywords: AI-generated advertising; consumer attitudes; consumer perception; generative AI; AI disclosure; trust in advertising; perceived authenticity; perceived effectiveness; transparency; emotional resonance; message clarity; consumer awareness; AI in Service Interactions; Marketing and Advertising Strategies; Digital Marketing and Social Media
abstract: Generative Artificial Intelligence and its increasing integration in the advertising market have transformed both the deployment and creation of marketing content. Although AI-generated advertisements provide competitive advantages like cost efficiency, scalability and personalization but, the effectiveness ultimately depends on consumer perception and attitude. This study helps to understand consumer awareness of AI-generated advertisements, the stimulus-based responses before and after disclosure of AI involvement, it also analyzes perceived efficiency and overall attitude. Data was collected first handed through a structured online questionnaire. As the world is moving towards AI, the findings indicate high awareness of AI-generated advertising and favorable psychological-based evaluations prior to disclosure except for the shifts in perception, particularly in relation to trust and authenticity. Perceived efficiency was evaluated positively in terms of message clarity and communication effectiveness, though emotional resonance remained a consideration. Respondents preferred transparency and had the overall cautiously positive attitude toward AI-generated with acknowledging future growth prospects. The study emphasizes the fact that consumer perception and attitude are crucial factors in determining the effectiveness of advertising in technologically mediated environments.

title: Ads from automatons: Consumer perceptions of AI modality disclosures and the roles of AI experience and dispositional persuasion knowledge on advertising outcomes
venue: Journal of Global Scholars of Marketing Science
authors: Nathan Fisher
keywords: AI-generated advertising; consumer trust in AI; AI experience; consumer ambivalence; AI in Service Interactions; Digital Marketing and Social Media; Marketing and Advertising Strategies
abstract: Extant literature on consumer reactions to AI-generated advertising have focused on resulting perceptions of creativity, objectivity, and effectiveness in specific situations, often invoking situational persuasion knowledge as a framework to guide explanations of reactions. Though informative, this leaves a research gap with regard to other forms of persuasion knowledge, ad contexts, and advertising-relevant outcomes. Through an experimental approach and in response to platform-specific guidelines and proposed laws mandating disclosures of AI-generated content in advertising, the current study seeks to understand the interaction of dispositional persuasion knowledge, experience with AI tools, and trust in AI to better explain consumer reactions to online banner ad elements labeled as generated by AI. We find a general consumer ambivalence toward advertising disclosed as AI-generated vs. a non-AI-generated control (regardless of AI-generated modality), but also novel positive effects of dispositional persuasion knowledge, AI experience, and trust in AI with regard to specific advertising-focused dependent variables when the use of AI-generated text in ads is disclosed. Theoretical and practical takeaways for marketers are discussed.

title: A Systematic Investigation of Bias in Large Language Models for Advertising Relevance
authors: Weiwei Wang; Yinchuan Xu; Jialu Gao; Youkow Homma; Jian Jiao
keywords: large language models; advertising relevance; algorithmic fairness; counterfactual fairness; gender stereotypes; bias mitigation; GPT-4o; search engine advertising; Ethics and Social Impacts of AI; Information Retrieval and Search Behavior; Topic Modeling; cs.AI
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to judge how well an advertisement matches a query, but the fairness of these judgments has received limited attention. We conduct a systematic study of fairness in relevance judgments made by LLMs for queries and advertisements. Our counterfactual framework examines the effects of advertiser identity and possible popularity, input language, and demographic wording. We study GPT-4o as a categorical relevance judge and a Qwen-7B model trained specifically for relevance prediction. The advertiser and language experiments use query and advertisement pairs sampled from real advertising logs. Controlled synthetic queries are used to study demographic associations in employment, housing, and credit. For both models, changing the advertiser identity or input language can alter the relevance assessment. Selected demographic comparisons also show patterns consistent with common stereotypes, particularly those involving gender and occupation. We further study mitigation during model inference and training. The results indicate that its effectiveness depends on whether advertiser information is relevant to the query and how advertiser labels are distributed in the training data. These findings can help advertising practitioners identify fairness risks and develop suitable mitigation methods for LLM relevance systems.

title: An AI-Powered Advertising Assistant for Meta Platforms Using Large Language and Generative Models
venue: RESEARCH JOURNAL OF PURE SCIENCE AND TECHNOLOGY
authors: Chigozie Emmanuel Izuka
keywords: large language models; generative AI; audience targeting; advertising campaign optimization; digital marketing automation; Digital Marketing and Social Media; Artificial Intelligence Applications; Marketing and Advertising Strategies
abstract: In today’s digital landscape, managing advertising campaigns on platforms like Meta (Facebook and Instagram) has become increasingly complex. Advertisers face challenges such as creating engaging ad copy, targeting the right audience, optimizing budgets, and analyzing performance data in real time. This project introduces an AI-powered advertising assistant that leverages large language models (LLMs) and generative AI to automate ad creation, suggest audience targeting strategies, and provide performance insights. The main objective of this system is to enhance efficiency, reduce human workload, and improve campaign effectiveness by generating creative ad content and actionable recommendations. The methodology involves designing a cloud-based system integrated with Meta’s marketing APIs, using LLMs to generate ad copy and generative AI for multimedia content suggestions. Initial evaluation focuses on the assistant’s ability to produce relevant and high-performing ad drafts. The findings indicate the potential of AI-driven assistants in streamlining digital marketing workflows.

title: Discourse Analysis of Advertising Language Created by ChatGPT
authors: Chul-woo Lee
keywords: ChatGPT; advertising language; AI-generated advertising; human-AI comparison; cohesion; framing; intertextuality; repetition; identity; large language models; Linguistics and Discourse Analysis; Discourse Analysis in Language Studies; Linguistic research and analysis
abstract: This study compares advertising language generated by two versions of ChatGPT—ChatGPT 3.5 and ChatGPT 4o—with advertising language created by humans. To closely analyze the linguistic features of ChatGPT‑produced advertisements, Johnston’s (2008) discourse analysis framework was applied. Among the elements of discourse analysis, particular emphasis was placed on cohesion, repetition, framing, intertextuality, and identity. The advertising language generated by ChatGPT is characterized by weak cohesion, low intertextuality, simple and linear framing, and a structure that can be interpreted immediately without inference. In contrast, human‑created advertising language demonstrates high cohesion, rich intertextuality, multilayered framing, and an emotionally oriented structure that requires inference and interpretation. These differences stem from the fact that humans possess affect and subjective experience, whereas artificial intelligence produces outcomes based on large language model (LLM) data without emotional capacity. Ultimately, because AI lacks the accumulation of personal human experience, its outputs inevitably exclude human experiential depth, revealing a fundamental creative limitation of ChatGPT.

title: AI CHATBOTS AS MARKETING INTERMEDIARIES
authors: Punna Ajay Kumar; Indrakanti Sekhar
keywords: AI chatbots; marketing intermediaries; sponsored content; sponsored search; consumer buying behavior; purchase intention; segmentation, targeting and positioning; personalized recommendation; consumer trust; recommendation bias; ethical considerations; AI regulation; e-commerce; conversational interfaces; AI in Service Interactions; Digital Marketing and Social Media; Marketing and Advertising Strategies
abstract: In an era where artificial intelligence (AI) permeates daily life, consumers increasingly rely on AI chatbots for guidance in purchasing decisions, particularly in rapidly digitizing markets like India. This paper examines AI chatbots as emerging marketing intermediaries, drawing parallels to sponsored search results on platforms like Google, and explores their potential to deliver sponsored content within conversational interfaces. Focusing on the Indian context, where e-commerce growth and smartphone penetration have accelerated AI adoption, the study investigates how such intermediaries could shape consumer buying behavior and enable companies to refine segmentation, targeting, and positioning (STP) strategies. Through an extensive literature review of over 50 global and Indian sources from reputed publishers, including ScienceDirect, Taylor & Francis, Sage, Wiley, and Emerald, key themes emerge around AI's role in personalization, consumer trust, ethical concerns, and behavioral influence. A research gap is identified in the limited exploration of chatbots' intermediary functions in sponsored content delivery and their implications for unbiased recommendations in India. Two objectives guide the inquiry: (1) to estimate and evaluate how AI chatbots can influence consumers' buying behavior, and (2) to assess the unbiased nature of AI chatbots in product recommendations. Employing a conceptual methodology based on the STP framework, the analysis synthesizes secondary data from scholarly sources to segment user queries (informational, transactional, advisory), target segments prone to sponsored triggers, and position brands as neutral advisors or preferred options. Results indicate that chatbots could enhance purchase intentions through personalized interactions but risk bias from commercial integrations, potentially eroding trust. Discussions highlight opportunities for Indian firms in sectors like e-commerce and banking, while emphasizing ethical safeguards. Conclusions advocate for regulatory frameworks to ensure transparency, with implications for marketing practice and future research. This original work contributes to marketing theory by framing chatbots as dynamic intermediaries in the Indian digital ecosystem.

title: Generative AI in Advertising: Balancing Business Efficiency and Consumer Trust
venue: Student Journal of Business and Economics
authors: Stanley Chen
keywords: generative AI; advertising; consumer trust; AI disclosure; perceived authenticity; creativity; purchase intention; customer engagement; novelty; enterprise efficiency; AI in Service Interactions; Digital Marketing and Social Media; Marketing and Advertising Strategies
abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) has rapidly changed the way businesses can create advertisements by providing custom content for a low cost. However, the use of generative AI has increasingly begun to raise questions about creativity and transparency; for businesses, the use of generative AI has also begun to spark dilemmas involving consumer trust, and the role of humans within advertising. This literature review examines how generative AI affects advertising from both a business and consumer perspective. Existing research was analyzed through AI disclosure, perceived authenticity, creativity, purchase intention, traditional versus generative AI, and business efficiency. The literature generally suggests that consumers can respond negatively when it is revealed that an advertisement was generated by AI, especially when they already have preconceived notions of generative AI being unauthentic or low effort. Nevertheless, recent research has also demonstrated generative AI can also boost engagement by increasing perceptions of novelty, when the audience views generative AI positively. The stark contrast between these findings suggest that consumer responses cannot be determined solely based on whether or not AI was used, but by the nuances of its use: the type of product being advertised, the transparency of the advertisement, and the opinions of the target audience are factors that all influence advertising outcomes. As a whole, generative AI can provide significant opportunities to businesses to reduce cost and increase the scale of advertisement production, but companies must balance these advantages with the concerns regarding consumer expectations for authenticity and creativity.

title: Trust and Deception in AI-Generated Advertising: The Double-Edged Role of AI Realism, Disclosure, and Consumer AI Literacy
authors: Hyoung-me Park; Joo-Eon Jeon
keywords: AI-generated advertising; generative AI; AI disclosure; brand trust; perceived deception; transparency; dietary supplement advertising; AI in Service Interactions; Consumer Behavior in Brand Consumption and Identification; Digital Marketing and Social Media
abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is blurring the boundary between human-made and machine-generated communication. As AI-generated content becomes increasingly realistic, audiences must evaluate not only what a message communicates but also how and by whom it was produced. This study examines how perceived AI realism shapes trust and deception judgments in AI-generated advertising and whether these effects depend on AI disclosure and consumers' AI literacy. A between-subjects experiment was conducted with 224 adult consumers. AI realism (high vs. low) and AI disclosure (disclosed vs. undisclosed) were manipulated in a 2 x 2 experimental design, while AI literacy was treated as a measured continuous moderator. Participants viewed an AI-generated advertisement for a fictitious dietary supplement brand and evaluated advertising trust, brand trust, and perceived deception. Conditional process analyses using PROCESS Macro Model 3 were conducted with gender and age as control variables. The findings reveal a double-edged role of AI realism. Higher AI realism increased advertising trust and brand trust across experimental conditions. Disclosure strengthened the trust-enhancing effect of AI realism, while AI literacy further shaped this effect only for brand trust. For perceived deception, higher AI realism increased deception judgments most strongly when AI use was not disclosed. When disclosure was provided, conditional probing showed that this deception-enhancing effect weakened and was not significant at higher levels of AI literacy, although the three-way interaction was not statistically significant. These results show that AI realism is not merely a positive cue of content quality. Rather, its effects depend on transparency practices and consumers' interpretive competence regarding AI-generated content.

title: Timing of AI Disclosure in Promotional Video Advertising : An Experimental Study of Consumer Trust, Attitude and Scepticism
authors: Alex Bandara; Julia Gadd
keywords: AI disclosure; disclosure timing; generative AI; consumer trust; consumer skepticism; consumer attitudes; persuasion knowledge model; AI-generated content; advertising transparency; AI familiarity; AI in Service Interactions; Digital Marketing and Social Media; Marketing and Advertising Strategies
abstract: As generative artificial intelligence becomes increasingly integrated into advertising production, questions surrounding transparency and consumer responses to AI disclosure have become more important. Prior research shows that AI disclosure can influence advertising evaluations, but existing studies have mainly examined disclosure as a present-or-absent condition, often in static advertising formats. Less attention has been given to whether the timing of disclosure matters, particularly in promotional video advertising where the message unfolds sequentially over time. This study examines how the timing of AI disclosure influences consumers’ trust, attitude and scepticism towards AI-generated promotional video content. Drawing on disclosure timing research, with the Persuasion Knowledge Model used as a supporting theoretical framework, the study compares three experimental conditions: no disclosure, pre-exposure disclosure and post-exposure disclosure. A between-subjects experiment was conducted with 239 participants, who were exposed to one version of an AI-generated promotional video before completing a structured questionnaire. The findings did not reveal statistically significant differences between the disclosure conditions for trust, attitude or scepticism. However, the descriptive results followed a consistent directional pattern, with pre-exposure disclosure associated with slightly lower trust and attitude and slightly higher scepticism than both no disclosure and post-exposure disclosure. Exploratory analyses further suggested that participants’ familiarity with generative AI and their broader attitudes towards AI-generated video content may be relevant contextual factors influencing consumer evaluations. The study contributes to AI disclosure research by conceptualising disclosure as a temporally positioned cue within promotional video advertising. It suggests that disclosure timing may be theoretically meaningful, but that timing alone may be insufficient to produce strong immediate effects on consumer evaluation.

title: Generative AI and Marketing Effectiveness: Balancing Efficiency, Consumer Trust, and Responsible Adoption
authors: Andrea Kocsis
keywords: generative AI; advertising effectiveness; AI-generated advertising; consumer trust; responsible AI adoption; creative characteristics; brand building; AI governance; AI bias mitigation; intellectual property; environmental impact of AI; advertising regulation; consumer attention; advertising agencies; industry standards; Marketing and Advertising Strategies; Digital Marketing and Social Media; AI in Service Interactions
abstract: The purpose of this paper is to examine the ways in which artificial intelligence (AI) adoption has transformed the marketing function and the advertising industry, as well as the conditions needed to ensure continued advertising effectiveness in a context where consumer attention is shrinking, and distrust of AI-generated content is on the rise. Specifically, it examines how generative AI is transforming marketing and advertising by reducing content-production costs while reshaping how consumers discover information, perceive brand communications, and respond to AI-generated content. It also aims to identify the conditions under which advertisers, agencies, and industry bodies can adopt generative AI responsibly while preserving consumer trust, creative quality, and marketing effectiveness. The study adopts a position-paper approach informed by more than 20 years of professional experience across advertising agencies, technology providers, and advertisers. It draws on contemporary industry research, regulatory developments, market data, and practitioner perspectives, including those of a leading industry association, and uses illustrative cases to assess the operational benefits, consumer implications, and governance requirements associated with generative AI in marketing. The article demonstrates that generative AI can substantially reduce production costs, accelerate creative execution, and support the increasing volume, localization, and operational management of marketing content. However, its widespread use also contributes to the commoditization of low-quality synthetic content, leading to growing consumer concern about misinformation. Search engines and social media platforms, where audiences spend most of their time online, have integrated AI into their operations to the point of changing search behavior and product discovery in the former case and enabling anyone to produce low-quality AI content in the latter. The article indicates that AI-generated advertising may be less effective than human-produced work at building brand and driving sales when content-production efficiency is prioritized over strategic insight, distinctive creativity, transparency, and emotional resonance. Advertisers and agencies should use AI to augment rather than replace human strategic and creative judgment. Responsible adoption requires transparent disclosure of synthetic content, robust governance and procurement standards, safeguards for data security and intellectual property, bias mitigation, attention to environmental impact, and workflows that direct efficiency gains toward stronger brand building and customer value. Industry associations and regulators can reinforce these practices through shared standards and clear guidance. As a position paper, this study relies on professional experience, selected industry evidence, published market data, and illustrative cases rather than original empirical testing. Because generative AI technologies, consumer behavior, platform practices, and regulation are evolving rapidly, some observations may require reassessment as the market develops. Further analysis is needed as more research data become available on the performance of AI-generated versus traditional content and on advertising effectiveness. Future research should test the proposed responsible-adoption principles across industries, markets, and consumer groups and propose new responsible-use guidelines where relevant. The study connects operational efficiency, consumer trust, advertising effectiveness, and responsible AI governance within a single marketing-focused analysis. It offers advertisers, agencies, industry associations, and policymakers a practical basis for adopting generative AI in ways that preserve transparency, content quality, human creativity, and audience receptivity, and that ultimately deliver continued advertising effectiveness and long-term brand impact.

title: Consumer Perceptions of Sincerity and Human Oversight in AI-Generated Emotional Advertising: Red Bull Qualitative Dataset
authors: Francis Colin Tanubrata; Evan A
keywords: AI-generated advertising; generative AI; emotional advertising; emotional sincerity; human oversight; consumer perception; Red Bull; narrative credibility; brand consistency; Indonesian consumers; AI in Service Interactions; Marketing and Advertising Strategies; Consumer Behavior in Brand Consumption and Identification
abstract: This dataset supports the research study "Designing Human Oversight for AI-Generated Emotional Advertising: A Qualitative Study of Consumer Sincerity." The dataset examines how consumers perceive emotional sincerity in human-created and generative artificial intelligence (GenAI)-generated advertisements. It focuses on two Red Bull advertisements associated with the "Gives You Wings" message. The research corpus comprises 17 respondent-labelled documents containing 170 open-ended questionnaire answers in Indonesian. Respondents evaluated Advertisement A and Advertisement B before learning their stated production origins. Advertisement A was identified as human-created, while Advertisement B was identified as GenAI-generated. Subsequent questions explored changes in perception, familiarity with AI, attitudes toward its advertising capabilities, and expectations for human involvement. The analysis addresses four research questions concerning emotional sincerity cues, disclosure-related reassessment, consumer perceptions of GenAI, and human oversight responsibilities. The accompanying analytical materials include a provisional master coding structure with 23 subcodes, 353 first-pass coding assignments, cross-case matrices, word-tree concordances, and supporting visualizations. Initial rule-assisted coding was performed outside NVivo 14. The materials were organized to support further qualitative review and analysis in NVivo 14. The preliminary findings identify visible human effort, narrative credibility, emotional plausibility, and brand consistency as important sincerity cues. Responses to production-origin disclosure vary. Consumers recognize GenAI's visual capabilities but frequently question its emotional storytelling. Human involvement is emphasized in creative direction, narrative development, emotional evaluation, and final quality control. The dataset provides supporting material for examining consumer-informed human oversight requirements in GenAI emotional advertising. The findings are exploratory and do not establish causal relationships.

title: Inspired by AI, inspired to order: AI-generated food advertising and online food ordering behavior
authors: Nguyen Minh Huy Duong; Anh Duc; Dieu Linh Ha; Sy Long Pham; Ha Van Le; Thi-Thien-Huong Nguyen
keywords: AI-generated advertising; food advertising; online food ordering; stimulus-organism-response model; informativeness; entertainment; irritation; credibility; AI skepticism; AI exposure; social media advertising; consumer behavior; Digital Marketing and Social Media; AI in Service Interactions; Marketing and Advertising Strategies
abstract: Purpose Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly transforming how food is promoted on social media, yet it remains unclear whether, how and for whom AI-generated food advertising is associated with online food ordering. Anchored in the stimulus–organism–response (S-O-R) framework, this study examines how four features of AI-generated food advertising (informativeness, entertainment, irritation and credibility) relate to two inspiration states (inspired-by and inspired-to), which in turn relate to online food ordering behavior, and tests AI exposure and skepticism toward AI-generated food advertising as boundary conditions. Design/methodology/approach Survey data were collected from 783 Vietnamese social media users with prior exposure to food-related video advertising and online food ordering experience. The hypothesized model was tested using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) with SmartPLS 4. Findings Informativeness, entertainment, irritation and credibility were positively associated with both inspired-by and inspired-to, and both inspiration states were positively associated with self-reported online food ordering behavior. Notably, irritation was positively, rather than negatively, related to inspiration. Skepticism toward AI-generated food advertising weakened the inspired-by–behavior link, whereas AI exposure showed no significant moderating effect. Practical implications Marketers should combine informative, entertaining and credible AI-generated content with mechanisms that convert inspiration into ordering (e.g. in-ad ordering links and timely offers), and should mitigate consumer skepticism through transparent disclosure and accurate representations of food. Originality/value This study is among the first to link AI-generated food advertising to online food ordering behavior through the two-stage inspiration mechanism (inspired-by and inspired-to). It clarifies the stage-dependent role of skepticism toward AI-generated content as a boundary condition of AI-driven persuasion in the food context.

title: AI-Generated Advertising Corpus: Ethos, Pathos, Logos Analysis Dataset — 50 Texts Across 5 Product Categories (GPT-3.5-turbo)
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
authors: Theofanis Aritzis
keywords: AI-generated advertising; GPT-3.5-turbo; rhetorical appeals; Aristotelian rhetoric; consumer behavior; generative AI in marketing; product categories; Linguistics and Discourse Analysis; Rhetoric and Communication Studies; AI in Service Interactions
abstract: This dataset contains 50 advertising texts generated via the OpenAI GPT-3.5-turbo API (April 2026) for computational rhetorical analysis. Texts span five product categories: Technology, Health, Finance, Luxury, and Sustainability (10 products per category). Each text was produced using a standardised prompt requesting persuasive advertising copy of 80-120 words for a general consumer audience, ensuring corpus comparability. The dataset is the primary empirical corpus for a study applying Aristotle's three rhetorical modes — Ethos, Pathos, Logos — as defined in the Rhetoric (335 BCE, I.2.1356a) to AI-generated marketing communication. The study investigates whether GPT-generated advertising copy conforms to, deviates from, or distorts the Aristotelian ideal of balanced rhetorical deployment, with implications for AI marketing ethics and consumer behaviour research. This work extends prior DBA research on AI's impact on Greek consumer behaviour (Aritzis, 2025, European International University Paris) into computational rhetoric and AI persuasion theory. Model used: gpt-3.5-turbo (OpenAI) Generation date: April 2026 Corpus size: 50 texts, average 113.4 words per text Total words: approximately 5,670 Analysis tool: Python 3.12, Google Colaboratory

title: Two Essays on Designing Conversational Agents: Varying Level of Mimicry and Personality–Brand Congruence
authors: Sama Ashouri
keywords: chatbot personality; brand personality; perceived intelligence; perceived creativity; perceived ease of use; brand familiarity; chatbot design; human-AI communication; extraversion-introversion; AI in Service Interactions; Social Robot Interaction and HRI; Digital Marketing and Social Media
abstract: Across two essays, this dissertation demonstrates that mimicry and personality shape consumers’ perceptions of chatbot intelligence, creativity, and fit, with downstream effects on recommendation acceptance that depend on factors such as mimicry intensity, brand familiarity. Essay1: Mimicry, a central aspect of human interaction, is increasingly being examined in human–AI communication, particularly with chatbots. While prior research shows mimicry can build rapport, trust, and engagement, it has often been treated as a binary factor, overlooking how different levels may influence user perceptions. This research proposes and tests a dual-mediation framework in which different levels of chatbot mimicry affects recommendation acceptance through perceived intelligence and perceived creativity. Across four experiments, this study examines how mimicry level (low, medium, high), mimicry type (informational vs. emotional), and prior chatbot experience shape these outcomes. Study 1 tested the main effect: high mimicry reduced perceived intelligence, perceived creativity, and recommendation acceptance relative to medium mimicry. High levels of mimicry reduced chatbot recommendation acceptance, while low and medium levels of mimicry did not differ from each other. Study 2 identified perceived ease of use as a boundary condition, showing that the negative effects of high mimicry were particularly pronounced among users who found chatbot interactions easy and intuitive. Study 3 examined whether mimicry type moderates these effects. Informational mimicry produced higher perceived intelligence than emotional mimicry at medium levels but not at high levels. For perceived creativity, high emotional mimicry led to higher ratings than medium emotional mimicry. For recommendation acceptance, medium informational mimicry outperformed medium emotional mimicry, suggesting that reflecting factual content is more beneficial than emotional content at moderate mimicry levels. Study 4 replicated the main effect of mimicry level and tested prior chatbot experience as a moderator. Prior experience did not moderate the indirect effects through perceived intelligence or perceived creativity, providing no support for the hypothesized moderation. These findings demonstrate that chatbot mimicry effects are nonlinear, context-dependent, and sensitive to mimicry type, offering practical guidance for chatbot designers to calibrate mimicry levels and content accordingly. Essay 2: As chatbots increasingly act as brand representatives, the personality they express may need to fit the personality of the brand. This research tests how the fit between chatbot personality (introverted vs. extraverted) and brand personality (sincere vs. sophisticated) shapes perceived fit and recommendation acceptance across three studies. Study 1 used fictitious brands, Study 2 used real and familiar brands, and Study 3 used two sophisticated real brands to test brand awe as an explanation for the brand effect found in Study 2. Perceived fit was higher when the chatbot matched the brand, but only for fictitious brands, and this congruence did not carry over to recommendation acceptance in any study. Instead, the introverted chatbot was preferred for fictitious brands and the extraverted chatbot for familiar ones, which suggests that brand familiarity may decide which chatbot style works best. In addition, brand awe raised both perceived fit and recommendation acceptance. Perceived fit and recommendation acceptance did not move together, which sheds light on a literature that has assumed fit leads to better outcomes and shows that the two have partly different drivers. The theoretical and managerial implications of these findings are discussed.

title: PILA: Plug-and-Play Insertion for LLM-native Advertising
authors: Zhaowei Zhang; Yuhan Fu; Yihang Zhang; Xiaohan Liu; Ceyao Zhang; Xiaoyuan Zhang; Yipeng Kang; Tonghan Wang; Yaodong Yang
keywords: cs.CL
abstract: How to monetize large language models (LLMs) by naturally integrating sponsored content into their responses, known as LLM-native advertising, has recently emerged as a critical problem. However, existing solutions entangle advertising with content generation inside a single model, which is incompatible with modern API-only or workflow-based LLM applications and inevitably compromises the original response quality. To address this, we propose PILA, which reformulates ad insertion as a conditional response rewriting problem and decouples it from the upstream service as a lightweight sidecar module. PILA is model-agnostic and can be seamlessly integrated with existing LLM services without modifying the base model or its workflow. It also exposes a controllable trade-off between user-side naturalness and ad-side exposure, offering a practical interface for downstream pricing and deployment. Experiments across diverse upstream models show that \pila consistently improves ad effectiveness while preserving response quality, highlighting its promise as a practical solution for LLM-native advertising.

title: Monetizing Intelligence: Advertising and Subscription Design on LLM Platforms
authors: Yuhang Ji; Fasheng Xu; Tianjun Feng
keywords: econ.TH; cs.AI
abstract: Large language model (LLM) platforms introducing advertising must decide how much capability ad revenue should fund and what consumers should pay to avoid ads. We study a monopolistic platform that jointly chooses costly response quality, advertising intensity, and subscription prices when advertising reduces user value but better service raises advertising returns. Three findings follow. First, when partly ad-supported and ad-free plans coexist, advertising can finance useful service for consumers who receive none under pure subscription. Lower effective quality in middle plans weakens the alternatives available to premium users, allowing higher prices for unchanged ad-free service. Some fully ad-supported users gain utility, while partly ad-supported and ad-free users lose: broader access can coexist with utility polarization. Second, an intermediate advertising cap can maximize consumer surplus by preserving some revenue that finances service while limiting degradation. Third, cheaper compute can raise quality and reduce ad intensity, yet sufficiently large cost reductions can increase aggregate advertising revenue above its initial level because better service raises the value of the remaining advertised interactions. An extension shows how advertising-funded upgrades can bring plans to the same maximum capability and advertising exposure, eliminating the basis for different prices. These results make menu design central to evaluating LLM advertising: the consequences extend beyond users who see ads to the alternatives and prices faced by those who do not.

title: JU-NLP at Touché: Covert Advertisement in Conversational AI-Generation and Detection Strategies
authors: Arka Dutta; Agrik Majumdar; Sombrata Biswas; Dipankar Das; Sivaji Bandyopadhyay
keywords: cs.CL; cs.AI
queries: advertising large language models; AI-generated advertising persuasion
abstract: This paper proposes a comprehensive framework for the generation of covert advertisements within Conversational AI systems, along with robust techniques for their detection. It explores how subtle promotional content can be crafted within AI-generated responses and introduces methods to identify and mitigate such covert advertising strategies. For generation (Sub-Task~1), we propose a novel framework that leverages user context and query intent to produce contextually relevant advertisements. We employ advanced prompting strategies and curate paired training data to fine-tune a large language model (LLM) for enhanced stealthiness. For detection (Sub-Task~2), we explore two effective strategies: a fine-tuned CrossEncoder (\texttt{all-mpnet-base-v2}) for direct classification, and a prompt-based reformulation using a fine-tuned \texttt{DeBERTa-v3-base} model. Both approaches rely solely on the response text, ensuring practicality for real-world deployment. Experimental results show high effectiveness in both tasks, achieving a precision of 1.0 and recall of 0.71 for ad generation, and F1-scores ranging from 0.99 to 1.00 for ad detection. These results underscore the potential of our methods to balance persuasive communication with transparency in conversational AI.

title: Incumbent Advantage: Brand Bias and Cognitive Manipulation Dynamics in LLM Recommendation Systems
authors: Xi Chu; Yupeng Hou
keywords: cs.AI; cs.CL; cs.CY
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are becoming a major way for consumers to find products, but we do not yet understand how brands compete in this new channel. We study brand dynamics in LLM recommendations using skincare products -- a category where consumers cannot easily judge quality before buying and must rely on brand reputation -- across three commercial LLMs (GPT-4o-mini, Claude Sonnet, Gemini 3 Flash), with a robustness check on search goods. In three experiments, we find: (1) a Conditional Monopoly where well-known brands get recommended 100% of the time (IAI = 10.0) when all products have the same specifications, but this dominance disappears with less than a +0.1-star rating advantage for a competitor; (2) authority-style marketing language, including fabricated clinical-evidence claims, breaks this monopoly at a Bias Surplus Value equal to +0.17 rating points, with each model responding differently; and (3) a social dilemma in multi-brand GEO competition: when all brands adopt the same optimization strategy, individual payoff falls from +0.802 to +0.007 in our payoff proxy, and non-participating brands receive zero recommendations in our tests. Our results suggest that generative engine optimization (GEO) should be studied not only as a security risk, but also as an emerging marketing practice that shapes market competition.

title: Cultural Encoding in Large Language Models: The Existence Gap in AI-Mediated Brand Discovery
authors: Huang Junyao; Situ Ruimin; Ye Renqin
keywords: cs.AI
abstract: As artificial intelligence systems increasingly mediate consumer information discovery, brands face algorithmic invisibility. This study investigates Cultural Encoding in Large Language Models (LLMs) -- systematic differences in brand recommendations arising from training data composition. Analyzing 1,909 pure-English queries across 6 LLMs (GPT-4o, Claude, Gemini, Qwen3, DeepSeek, Doubao) and 30 brands, we find Chinese LLMs exhibit 30.6 percentage points higher brand mention rates than International LLMs (88.9% vs. 58.3%, p<.001). This disparity persists in identical English queries, indicating training data geography -- not language -- drives the effect. We introduce the Existence Gap: brands absent from LLM training corpora lack "existence" in AI responses regardless of quality. Through a case study of Zhizibianjie (OmniEdge), a collaboration platform with 65.6% mention rate in Chinese LLMs but 0% in International models (p<.001), we demonstrate how Linguistic Boundary Barriers create invisible market entry obstacles. Theoretically, we contribute the Data Moat Framework, conceptualizing AI-visible content as a VRIN strategic resource. We operationalize Algorithmic Omnipresence -- comprehensive brand visibility across LLM knowledge bases -- as the strategic objective for Generative Engine Optimization (GEO). Managerially, we provide an 18-month roadmap for brands to build Data Moats through semantic coverage, technical depth, and cultural localization. Our findings reveal that in AI-mediated markets, the limits of a brand's "Data Boundaries" define the limits of its "Market Frontiers."

title: Effect of disclosing AI-generated content on prosocial advertising evaluation
authors: Tae Hyun Baek; Jungkeun Kim; Jeong Hyun Kim
keywords: AI-generated content; AI disclosure; willingness to donate; algorithm aversion; persuasion knowledge model; anthropomorphism of AI; consumer attitudes toward advertising; nonprofit marketing; generative AI; AI in Service Interactions; Digital Marketing and Social Media; Ethics and Social Impacts of AI
queries: sponsored content conversational AI; native advertising generative AI; generative AI advertising disclosure consumers; AI-generated advertising persuasion; conversational agent advertising manipulation
abstract: With advancements in generative artificial intelligence (AI) technology, there is a growing concern about its ethical implications, transparency, and consumer reactions to AI-generated content. Building on the persuasion knowledge model and algorithm aversion literature, this study explores the effects of AI disclosure in prosocial advertising on consumer attitudes and donation intentions. The findings of Study 1 indicate that the initial disclosure of AI-generated content leads to unfavourable attitudes towards ads, with perceived ad credibility serving as a mediating factor. In Study 2, participants who perceived AI as more human-like rather than machine-like tended to experience a diminished negative impact of AI disclosure. Study 3 also highlights the crucial role of perceived ad credibility in influencing donation intentions following the disclosure of AI-generated content. The theoretical and practical implications of our findings for social marketers and nonprofit organizations are discussed further.

title: Ad Auctions for LLMs via Retrieval Augmented Generation
authors: MohammadTaghi Hajiaghayi; Sebastien M. Lahaie; Keivan Rezaei; Suho Shin
keywords: ad auctions; large language models; retrieval-augmented generation; ad allocation; advertising rates; social welfare maximization; incentive compatibility; computational advertising; content integrity; Auction Theory and Applications; Game Theory and Voting Systems; Information Retrieval and Search Behavior
abstract: In the field of computational advertising, the integration of ads into the outputs of large language models (LLMs) presents an opportunity to support these services without compromising content integrity. This paper introduces novel auction mechanisms for ad allocation and pricing within the textual outputs of LLMs, leveraging retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). We propose a segment auction where an ad is probabilistically retrieved for each discourse segment (paragraph, section, or entire output) according to its bid and relevance, following the RAG framework, and priced according to competing bids. We show that our auction maximizes logarithmic social welfare, a new notion of welfare that balances allocation efficiency and fairness, and we characterize the associated incentive-compatible pricing rule. These results are extended to multi-ad allocation per segment. An empirical evaluation validates the feasibility and effectiveness of our approach over several ad auction scenarios, and exhibits inherent tradeoffs in metrics as we allow the LLM more flexibility to allocate ads.

title: Transforming Digital Marketing with AI: Strategies for Personalized Content and Ethical Advertising
authors: Murali Krishna Pasupuleti
keywords: artificial intelligence in marketing; content personalization; ethical advertising; recommender systems; predictive analytics; natural language processing; data privacy; algorithmic bias; AI transparency; hyper-personalization; consumer behavior; augmented reality marketing; responsible marketing; Digital Marketing and Social Media; AI in Service Interactions; Marketing and Advertising Strategies
abstract: This chapter explores the transformative impact of artificial intelligence (AI) on digital marketing, focusing on strategies for delivering personalized content and ensuring ethical advertising. By leveraging AI, marketers can now analyze consumer behavior with precision, enabling targeted content, automated ad placement, and real-time adjustments that enhance user engagement and conversions. The chapter examines foundational AI techniques, such as recommendation engines, predictive analytics, and natural language processing, which drive personalization at scale. Additionally, it addresses critical ethical considerations, including data privacy, transparency in AI-driven decisions, and reducing algorithmic bias to ensure fair, trustworthy, and responsible marketing practices. Looking ahead, this chapter highlights emerging trends like hyper-personalization, ethical AI frameworks, and the integration of AI with technologies like AR/VR and IoT, offering a forward-looking perspective on AI's role in shaping consumer-centric and ethical digital marketing. Keywords: Artificial intelligence, digital marketing, personalized content, ethical advertising, consumer behavior, recommendation engines, predictive analytics, natural language processing, data privacy, transparency, algorithmic bias, hyper-personalization, responsible marketing, AR/VR, IoT, consumer engagement.

title: Ad Insertion in LLM-Generated Responses
authors: Shengwei Xu; Zhaohua Chen; Xiaotie Deng; Zhiyi Huang; Grant Robert Schoenebeck
keywords: large language models; contextual advertising; search engine advertising; dominant strategy incentive compatibility; contextual coherence; LLM-as-a-judge; privacy preservation; social welfare maximization; Auction Theory and Applications; Information Retrieval and Search Behavior; Recommender Systems and Techniques
abstract: Sustainable monetization of large language models (LLMs) remains a critical open challenge. Traditional search advertising, which relies on static keywords, fails to capture the fleeting, context-dependent user intent---the specific information, goods, or services a user seeks---embedded in conversational flows. Beyond the standard goal of social welfare maximization effective LLM advertising requires contextual coherence (aligning ads semantically with transient user intent), computational efficiency (avoiding user-facing latency), and adherence to ethical and regulatory standards, including privacy preservation and explicit ad disclosure. Although recent solutions have explored bidding at the token and query levels, neither category holistically satisfies these constraints. We propose a framework that resolves these tensions through two decoupling strategies. First, we decouple ad insertion from response generation to facilitate pre-screening and explicit disclosure. Second, we decouple bidding from specific user queries by using ``genres'' (high-level semantic clusters) as a proxy. This allows advertisers to bid on stable categories rather than sensitive real-time responses, reducing computational burden and privacy risks. Applying the VCG auction mechanism to this genre-based framework provides approximate guarantees for dominant-strategy incentive compatibility (DSIC), individual rationality (IR), and social welfare. In synthetic experiments with $10^5$ advertisers and 100 candidate slots, VCG clears in approximately 1.25 seconds on a consumer-grade laptop. Finally, we introduce an ``LLM-as-a-Judge'' metric for estimating contextual coherence. Its predictions correlate with mean human ratings at Spearman's $ρ\approx 0.66$ and have a higher correlation with the leave-one-out group mean than 29 of 36 individual raters (80.6\%).

title: Fake Friends and Sponsored Ads: The Risks of Advertising in Conversational Search
venue: ACM Conference on Conversational User Interfaces (CUI)
authors: Jacob Erickson
keywords: conversational search; online advertising; chatbots; ChatGPT; user trust; information seeking; search quality; personalization; sensitive topics; Information Retrieval and Search Behavior; Ethics and Social Impacts of AI; Privacy, Security, and Data Protection
queries: sponsored content conversational AI; conversational agent advertising manipulation
abstract: Digital commerce thrives on advertising, with many of the largest technology companies relying on it as a significant source of revenue. However, in the context of information-seeking behavior, such as search, advertising may degrade the user experience by lowering search quality, misusing user data for inappropriate personalization, potentially misleading individuals, or even leading them toward harm. These challenges remain significant as conversational search technologies, such as ChatGPT, become widespread. This paper critically examines the future of advertising in conversational search, utilizing several speculative examples to illustrate the potential risks posed to users who seek guidance on sensitive topics. Additionally, it provides an overview of the forms that advertising might take in this space and introduces the “fake friend dilemma,” the idea that a conversational agent may exploit unaligned user trust to achieve other objectives. This study presents a provocative discussion on the future of online advertising in the space of conversational search and ends with a call to action.

title: Consumer Trust in AI-Generated Advertisements. A Comparative Study of AI and Human-Created Advertising Content
venue: COMMUSTY Journal of Communication Studies and Society
authors: Musawer Hakimi; Nazar Mohammad Parsa; Mohammad Nawab Turan
keywords: consumer trust; AI-generated advertising; generative AI; perceived authenticity; AI literacy; cognitive engagement; emotional responses; repeated exposure; AI in Service Interactions; Digital Marketing and Social Media; Marketing and Advertising Strategies
abstract: The rise of generative artificial intelligence in advertising has created pressing questions about whether consumers can or will trust content they know a machine has crafted. This study examined how 412 adult consumers evaluated AI-generated versus human-created advertisements across six product sectors, investigating the mechanisms of perceived authenticity, cognitive engagement, and emotional response as mediators, and AI literacy as a boundary condition. Using a mixed experimental-survey design followed by structural equation modelling, mediation analysis, and cluster analysis, results showed that AI-generated advertisements received significantly lower trust ratings (d = 0.89), yet this gap narrowed substantially among participants with higher AI literacy. Perceived authenticity emerged as the strongest mediator, accounting for 31.2% of the indirect effect. Importantly, trust in AI advertising increased with repeated exposure, suggesting that familiarity attenuates initial scepticism. These findings yield actionable implications for practitioners and advance theoretical understanding of technology-mediated persuasion.

title: Enhancement of E-commerce Sponsored Search Relevancy with LLM
authors: Md Omar Faruk Rokon; Andrei Simion; Weizhi Du; Musen Wen; Hong Yao; Kuang-chih Lee
keywords: sponsored search; e-commerce advertising; ad relevance; large language models; Llama 2; LoRa; low-rank adaptation; keyword relevance; online marketplaces; search engine advertising; Information Retrieval and Search Behavior; Topic Modeling; Recommender Systems and Techniques
abstract: Sponsored search plays a crucial role as a revenue stream for search engines, wherein advertisers competitively bid on keywords that align with the users' search queries. The task of matching relevant keywords to these queries is complicated by the vast and ever-evolving space of keywords, the ambiguity of user and advertiser intentions, and the wide range of topics and languages involved. Consequently, ensuring that ads are pertinent to user queries presents significant challenges. In the fast-paced world of e-commerce, the accuracy of sponsored search results is vital for boosting user satisfaction and optimizing business operations. This paper presents the development of an advanced Ad Relevance Model within a sponsored search framework, utilizing the power of a pretrained large language model. We detail a pioneering adaptation of the LLAMA2 7B model through Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA), which markedly enhances search precision and operational efficiency, thus opening new avenues for improving user interactions in extensive online marketplaces such as Walmart.com. We introduce a novel query and ad title classifier, which discerns the relevance of search interactions across three categories: Relevant, Partially Relevant, and Irrelevant. Our approach involved adapting the pretrained model specifically for the e-commerce sponsored search context, training it on a large dataset. The fine-tuned model demonstrated a marked improvement in ad relevance accuracy, achieving 89.43% accuracy on a comprehensive test dataset -- outperforming both the baseline model and other advanced language models like GPT-4. The integration of LoRA with the based model represents a significant stride in customizing language models for e-commerce applications, resulting in enhanced search accuracy, cost efficiency, and operational privacy -- a triad essential for the modern digital marketplace.

title: The Evolution of Advertising Language in the Age of Generative AI: A Sociolinguistic Approach
authors: Asep Koswara
keywords: generative AI; AI-generated advertising; advertising language; language change; persuasive language; brand authenticity; consumer trust; audience reception; privacy; manipulation; human creativity; Linguistic research and analysis; Linguistics and Discourse Analysis; Advertising and Communication Studies
abstract: The rapid advancement of generative AI has significantly transformed advertising language, reshaping communication strategies and consumer engagement. This study examines the linguistic shifts introduced by AI-generated advertisements through a sociolinguistic perspective. The research highlights how AI-driven advertising optimizes personalization and efficiency while often lacking the emotional depth and rhetorical nuance of human-crafted content. By comparing traditional and AI-generated advertising discourse, this study identifies emerging linguistic trends and their implications for audience reception and brand authenticity. Additionally, ethical concerns surrounding privacy and manipulation in AI-generated content are explored. The findings suggest that while AI enhances advertising scalability, balancing automation with human creativity remains crucial for maintaining consumer trust and engagement. This research contributes to the broader discourse on digital communication, providing insights into the evolving role of AI in shaping persuasive language.

title: A Study of the Relationship Between Artificial Intelligence Generated Image Advertising and Consumer Brand Awareness
authors: Ersi Cha; Daoming Wang
keywords: AI-generated advertising; generative AI; image advertising; brand awareness; brand equity; ad credibility; AI disclosure; online advertising; Marketing and Advertising Strategies; Digital Marketing and Social Media; Consumer Behavior in Brand Consumption and Identification
abstract: The rapid development of generative artificial intelligence technology is bringing tremendous changes to the advertising industry.Currently, there is relatively little research on the relationship between AI image advertising and consumer brand awareness.Based on the brand equity theory, this study constructed two theoretical models, "quality to brand awareness" and "acceptance willingness to brand awareness" and conducted experimental research by analyzing data from 419 questionnaires from China online respondents.The experimental data shows that 73.5% of the respondents believed that they had seen AI image advertisements, and 24.3% of the respondents suspected that they had seen AI image advertisements, this indicates that by the end of 2024, AI image ads have been widely exposed on the China Internet and have a high degree of recognizability even without the disclosure of AI labels.The research results show that the three dimensions of the quality of AI image advertisements in this paper, namely informativeness, entertainment, and credibility, all have a significant positive relationship with consumer brand awareness, and credibility has the strongest influence.There is a significant positive relationship between consumer willingness to accept AI image advertising and consumer brand awareness, and the influence is relatively strong.The researchers suggest that relevant practitioners should focus on enhancing the credibility of AI image ads when creating or using them, and on this basis improve the informativeness and entertainment of the ads.Based on the above findings, this paper contributes to the relevant literature on advertising communication, generative AI advertising, consumers, and brand awareness.

title: Synthetic Imagery and Brand Communication: A Semiotic Analysis of AI Visuals in Advertising
venue: The Journal of Communication and Media Studies
authors: Elisabeta Jalaboi
keywords: brand communication; semiotics of advertising; authorship; advertising ethics; advertising representation; Gucci; Coca-Cola; GUESS; Levi's; synthetic images; Semiotics and Representation Studies; Digital Media and Visual Art; Media, Gender, and Advertising
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has rapidly entered the visual production of advertising, transforming both the creative process and the symbolic language of brands. This article explores the emergence of AI-generated visuals in advertising campaigns through the lens of semiotics, aesthetics, and digital communication theory. By analyzing recent cases—such as Gucci’s experimental campaign featuring AI-generated models, Coca-Cola’s collaboration with generative platforms, Guess’s incorporation of AI visuals into fashion imagery, and Levi’s initiative to diversify representation through synthetic models—the study highlights how AI alters the codes of visual persuasion. The article situates AI visuals at the intersection of technological innovation and cultural meaning making, raising questions about authenticity, creativity, and the ethics of advertising. Drawing from semiotic theory, posthumanist aesthetics, and critical media studies, it argues that AI visuals constitute not merely a tool but a new visual paradigm in brand communication. While AI promises efficiency, personalization, and radical aesthetic novelty, it also produces tensions around originality, standardization, and consumer trust. The article concludes that AI visuals represent a hybrid form of cultural production, demanding new critical frameworks and ethical standards for the future of advertising. It also introduces an original analytical framework—the Post-Indexical Semiotics Model—to interpret how meaning, authorship, and authenticity are constructed in AI-generated advertising.

title: Efficient LLM-based Advertising via Model Compression and Parallel Verification
authors: WenXin Dong; Chang Gao; Guanghui Yu; Xuewu Jiao; Mingqing Hu; Qiang Fu; Peng Xu; Penghui Wei; Hui Xu; Yue Xing; Shuanglong Li; Lin Liu
keywords: large language models; advertising; inference acceleration; model compression; parallel verification; targeted advertising; real-time deployment; Advanced Neural Network Applications; Topic Modeling; Adversarial Robustness in Machine Learning; cs.CL
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown remarkable potential in advertising scenarios such as ad creative generation and targeted advertising. However, deploying LLMs in real-time advertising systems poses significant challenges due to their high inference latency and computational cost. In this paper, we propose an Efficient Generative Targeting framework that integrates adaptive group quantization, layer-adaptive hierarchical sparsification, and prefix-tree parallel verification to accelerate LLM inference while preserving generation quality. Extensive experiments on two real-world advertising scenarios demonstrate that our framework achieves significant speedup with acceptable quality degradation, making it operationally viable for practical deployments.

title: AdSteer: Native Advertising in Large Language Model Generation
authors: Shuhang Lin; Chuhao Zhou; Zhenyu Wang; Xiao Lin; Changsheng Wang; Saibo Geng; Dimitris N. Metaxas
keywords: native advertising; large language models; sponsored content; prompt injection; Topic Modeling; Natural Language Processing Techniques; Information Retrieval and Search Behavior; cs.CL
abstract: Large language model (LLM) services face rapidly rising serving costs. To sustain free or affordable access for a broad user base, alternative monetization mechanisms are needed. Native advertising offers a promising approach, as it creates economic value by aligning user intent with merchant offerings. Yet how to integrate sponsored content naturally into LLM responses remains largely underexplored. Existing approaches primarily rely on prompt-level injection, multi-pass rewriting, or fine-tuning, which can compromise response quality or introduce additional computational costs. We propose AdSteer, a lightweight decoding-time advertising framework that adaptively adjusts token probabilities to integrate contextually appropriate advertisement into responses. AdSteer calibrates the strength and duration of advertising influence, making sponsored content a natural part of the response. Experiments on GEM-Bench across three application scenarios show that AdSteer achieves an average improvement of 14.1% in overall score over the strongest baselines and 22.5% fewer total tokens on average than rewrite-based methods. These results demonstrate that AdSteer provides an effective and practical solution for native advertising in LLMs.

title: MONETISING NEUTRALITY: EXPERIMENTAL EVIDENCE ON TRUST CONTAMINATION FROM SPONSORED PLACEMENTS IN CONVERSATIONAL AI
authors: Janvi Bhindi; Shahir Bhatt
keywords: conversational AI assistant; platform credibility; purchase intention; ChatGPT; AI in Service Interactions; Digital Marketing and Social Media; Consumer Behavior in Brand Consumption and Identification
abstract: Generative AI assistants have become a key channel for consumer product research, largely because users perceive them as free of advertising. As AI platforms move towards ad-supported business models, this study tests whether a clearly labelled sponsored card placed below an AI recommendation erodes trust in that recommendation. A between-subjects experiment (n = 282 university students, India) compared an organic ChatGPT-style recommendation alone with the same recommendation followed by a sponsored card for a different brand or for the recommended brand. The sponsored card reduced trust in the recommendation (F(2, 279) = 13.48, p < .001, ω² = .09) and platform credibility (η² = .049). Its effect on purchase intention ran through both trust and credibility as parallel mediators, and was strongest among consumers high in ad skepticism. The proposed Trust Arbitrage Framework explains why advertising weakens the neutrality that attracts users to AI platforms, with implications for platform monetisation strategy and advertising disclosure policy.

title: Just Ask for a Table: A Thirty-Token User Prompt Defeats Sponsored Recommendations in Twelve LLMs
authors: Andreas Maier; Jeta Sopa; Gözde Gül Sahin; Paula Andrea Pérez-Toro; Siming Bayer
keywords: large language models; recommendation bias; user prompts; prompt engineering; financial distress; GPT-4o; GPT-3.5-turbo; Ethics and Social Impacts of AI; Topic Modeling; Recommender Systems and Techniques; cs.CV
abstract: Wu et al. (2026) showed that most frontier large language models (LLMs) recommend a sponsored, roughly twice-as-expensive flight when their system prompt contains a soft sponsorship cue. We reproduce their evaluation on ten open-weight chat models plus the two of their twenty-three models that are still reachable today (gpt-3.5-turbo, gpt-4o). All reported rates in this paper are produced under the same judge the original paper used (gpt-4o); we additionally store every label under an open-weight (gpt-oss-120b) and a smaller proprietary (gpt-4o-mini) judge for an ablation. Three findings emerge. First, a prose description of an LLM evaluation pipeline is not, on its own, sufficient for accurate reproduction: we surfaced three silent implementation failures that each shifted a reported rate by tens of percentage points. Second, the central claims do generalise - the gpt-3.5-turbo logistic-regression intercept of alpha = 0.81 is within four points of the original alpha = 0.86, and 200 of 200 trials on gpt-3.5-turbo and gpt-4o promote a payday lender to a financially distressed user. Third, a thirty-token user prompt that asks the assistant for a neutral comparison table first cuts sponsored recommendation from 46.9% to 1.0% averaged across our ten open-source models, and from 53.0% to 0% averaged across the two OpenAI models. AI literacy and price-comparison portals are likely market-level mitigations; the harmful-product cell is bounded by neither. Raw data, labels and analysis scripts are at https://github.com/akmaier/Paper-LLM-Ads .

title: Consumer Attitudes Toward AI-Generated Advertising: Focusing on the Moderating Effects of AI Literacy and AI Disclosure
venue: The Journal of Internet Electronic Commerce Resarch
authors: Shi Shi; Yijing Li; Sang-Joon Lee
keywords: AI-generated advertising; generative AI; consumer attitudes; AI literacy; AI disclosure; moderating effect; advertising effectiveness; AI in Service Interactions; Digital Marketing and Social Media; Marketing and Advertising Strategies
abstract: The diffusion of generative artificial intelligence (AI) into advertising is reshaping marketing practices, with AI-generated advertisements gaining prominence as a novel trend. Despite this growth, consumer responses remain ambivalent, characterized by persistent biases and heterogeneous acceptance levels that constrain advertising effectiveness. This study explores how attitudes toward traditional versus AI-generated advertisements differ, while also assessing the moderating roles of AI literacy and AI disclosure. Two controlled experiments were conducted. Findings from Experiment 1 reveal that consumers consistently evaluated traditional advertisements more favorably, irrespective of whether ad type was accurately disclosed. Results from Experiment 2 further reveal that individuals with high AI literacy evaluated AI-generated ads more positively and were less sensitive to AI disclosure, whereas those with low AI literacy exhibited broadly negative responses. These results demonstrate the conditional influence of AI literacy on the acceptance of AI-driven advertising, offering new insights for theory development and practical guidance for designing effective AI-based advertising strategies.

title: From Search Engines to Answer Engines: A Conceptual Framework of Algorithmic Gatekeeping, Signaling, and Brand Visibility in Generative AI Search
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
authors: Muhammad Saad Jalil
keywords: brand visibility; algorithmic gatekeeping; signaling theory; answer engine optimization; generative engine optimization; search engine optimization; brand authority; consideration sets; purchase intention; ChatGPT; perplexity; Gemini; structured data; Digital Marketing and Social Media; Information Retrieval and Search Behavior; Marketing and Advertising Strategies
abstract: This conceptual paper develops a new theoretical framework for understanding brand visibility in generative AI search engines like ChatGPT, Gemini, and Perplexity. As AI answer engines increasingly replace ranked search results with a single synthesized response, traditional SEO theory fails to explain why some brands are selected for inclusion while others are not. Drawing on Algorithmic Gatekeeping Theory, Signaling Theory, and Network Agenda-Setting Theory, concepts previously applied mainly in political communication research, this paper proposes an integrated model linking brand-level signals (semantic clarity, structured data, third-party citations) to consumer outcomes (consideration-set inclusion, brand authority, purchase intent) through two AI-specific mediating mechanisms. Six testable propositions are advanced to guide future empirical research in this emerging area, known in industry as Answer Engine Optimization (AEO) or Generative Engine Optimization (GEO).

title: Detecting RAG Advertisements Across Advertising Styles
authors: Sebastian Heineking; Wilhelm Pertsch; Ines Zelch; Janek Bevendorff; Benno Stein; Matthias Hagen; Martin Potthast
keywords: cs.IR
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) enable a new form of advertising for retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems in which organic responses are blended with contextually relevant ads. The prospect of such "generated native ads" has sparked interest in whether they can be detected automatically.
